nodes.title: Guide to Constrained Maximization
GUIDE TO PERFORM CONSUMER MAXIMIZATION
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{APPLICATION: Consumer Problem vs CE --- same recipe}}

1) Setup (+ decide which constraints bind), 2) Lagrangian, 3) FOCs by good (one per choice variable), 4) Merge FOCs, 5) Merge FOCs into BC $\to$ Marshallian, 6) in CE apply market clearing.
\begin{tabular}{p{4.5cm}|p{18cm}|p{18cm}}
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Consumer Problem (1 agent)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Competitive Equilibrium ($H$ agents)}} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1)} \emph{Setup: max problem, choice variables, constraints + decide which bind.} &
$$ \boxed{\;\max_{x}\; U(x)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad p\cdot x \le w\ (\lambda),\qquad x_i \ge 0\ (\mu_i)\ \forall i.\;} $$
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Choice variables:}} $x=(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ --- $N$ variables; $p,w$ \emph{given / exogenous}.
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} Budget binds for sure (strict monotonicity $\Rightarrow\lambda>0$, CS $\Rightarrow p\cdot x^*=w$: \textbf{ALWAYS an equality}). $x_i\ge0$ slack for sure under Inada ($x_i^*>0\Rightarrow\mu_i=0$ by CS); \textcolor{orange}{no Inada (e.g.\ QL) $\Rightarrow$ TO BE TESTED}.
\textcolor{green}{Comment: at the setup you already ask WHICH constraints bind. If clear from Inada / monotonicity, pick and go on. If in doubt, write the two possibilities (interior / non-interior), start interior and, if the ex-post check disproves it, re-solve at the corner --- the TRIAL step of the standard KKT template.}
 & 
$$ \boxed{\;\max_{x^h}\; U^h(x^h)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad p\cdot x^h \le p\cdot\omega^h\ (\lambda^h),\qquad x_i^h \ge 0\ (\mu_i^h),\qquad h=1,\dots,H.\;} $$
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Choice variables:}} the bundles $\{x^h\}_{h=1}^{H}$ --- $N\cdot H$ variables; \textcolor{orange}{wealth $w^h=p\cdot\omega^h$ ENDOGENOUS}.
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} Each budget BINDS BY MONOTONICITY ($\lambda^h>0$); $x_i^h\ge0$ DOES NOT BIND BY INADA (EXCEPT QL preferences $\to$ test ex post).
 \\
\hline
\textbf{(2)} \emph{Lagrangian --- one multiplier per constraint.} & Lagrangian (one budget $\to$ one $\lambda$):
$$ \mathcal{L} = U(x) + \lambda\bigl[\,w - p \cdot x\,\bigr]. $$ & Each agent $h = 1, \ldots, H$ solves \emph{their own} consumer problem with their own multiplier $\lambda^h$ (one budget $\to$ one $\lambda^h$):
$$ \mathcal{L}^h = U^h(x^h) + \lambda^h\bigl[\,p\cdot\omega^h - p\cdot x^h\,\bigr]. $$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(3)} \emph{FOCs --- one per choice variable, by good.} & \textcolor{blue}{One agent, $N$ choice variables} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$N$ FOCs}.
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{One FOC per good $i$:}}
$$ \boxed{\;\tfrac{\partial U(x^*)}{\partial x_i} = \underbrace{\lambda}_{\text{from the BC}}\, p_i \;\;\forall i = 1,\ldots,N.\;} $$
\emph{$N$ equations, each pinning down one $x_i^*$.}

{{img:2|w=680}} 

Notice what $\lambda$ is! $\lambda$ is the marginal value of relaxing the BC!! extremely interesting the lhs is equated to this. "Why one λ": one budget constraint ⇒ one shadow price. An agent has a single pot of wealth, so there's a single scarcity price on it, and every good must earn that same return per dollar at the margin (COMMON, not "EXOGENOUS"). This also explains the cross-agent side of the right plot (the CE) perfectly: each agent has their own budget constraint. There is a within agent unification in bang for buck! 
If $\frac{MU_a}{p_a} > \frac{MU_b}{p_b}$, moving one dollar of spending from $B$ to $A$ raises utility (for the same dollar spent). So at an optimum no such move can be profitable ⇒ bang-for-buck must be equal across all goods. & \textcolor{blue}{$H$ agents, each with $N$ choice variables} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$N \cdot H$ FOCs}.
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{One FOC per good $i$ AND per agent $h$:}}
$$ \boxed{\;\tfrac{\partial U^h(x^{h*})}{\partial x_i^h} = \lambda^h\, p_i \;\;\forall i = 1, \ldots, N,\;\; \forall h = 1, \ldots, H.\;} $$
\emph{$N \cdot H$ equations: $N$ per agent, $H$ agents.}

this is an extrenely deep optimality condition. at the optimum everyone will consume untile th emarginal utility is equal to the marginal value of an extra unit for society = the price! Note two sophistications: 1) the price is endogenous, dpends on endowments and what the others want to do and 2) the convergence is a market dynamic: those who have higher demand (higher mu) will buy, the others will sell! 

THIS EXPLANATION FOR THE PRICE makes it even cleaner the role of the planner multipleirs. in this case, the social value of +1u of consumption is emerging naturally from the market. you do not need a planner to allcoate, but just need agents to buy and sell!

{{img:1|w=680}}
This plot is the counterpart of the FOC optimality conditions: 1) the focs are a within agent condition; and 2) it is obvious the MU cannot easily be the same across agents. Note here we have agents with heterogeneous utility functions! \\
\hline
\textbf{(4)} \emph{Merge FOCs (take ratios) $\to$ optimality condition.} & The famous optimality condition: Taking ratios of FOC$_i$ / FOC$_j$ eliminates $\lambda$:
$\underbrace{\dfrac{\partial U/\partial x_i}{\partial U/\partial x_j}}_{\substack{\text{MRS}_{i,j} = \text{internal exchange rate}\\ = -\,\text{slope indiff.\ curve}\;(\dagger,\ddagger)}} = \underbrace{\dfrac{p_i}{p_j}}_{-\,\text{slope budget}}.$

{{img:0|w=380}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{$N$-dimensional MRS.}} With $N$ goods, MRS is \emph{not} a single number --- it's a \textcolor{orange}{family of pairwise ratios}:
$$ \text{MRS}_{i,j} := \dfrac{\partial U/\partial x_i}{\partial U/\partial x_j}, \quad \text{total of } \binom{N}{2} = \tfrac{N(N-1)}{2} \text{ pairs.} $$
Optimality: \emph{every} pair satisfies $\text{MRS}_{i,j} = p_i/p_j$. Equivalently, \textcolor{orange}{all $N$ ratios $MU_i / p_i$ are equal}, with common value $\lambda$ (the multiplier). Note how when within agent liens touch thism eans ther eis no longer and incentive to trade x for y because the dollar MB is unified! & Same condition for each agent. Since the RHS is \emph{common} across agents (everyone faces the same prices):
$$ \boxed{\;\text{MRS}^1 = \text{MRS}^2 = \cdots = \text{MRS}^H = \tfrac{p_i}{p_j}.\;} $$
\textcolor{orange}{MRS equalization across all agents at CE.}
This, again, means they optimized against the same ratio of prices. Plus, it also means no profitable exchange is left. \\
\hline
\textbf{(5)} \emph{Substitute FOCs into the binding BC $\to$ Marshallian demand.} & \underline{Substitute} the FOC ratios into the binding BC equation and get:
$$ \boxed{\;x_i^* = x_i^*(p, w)\;} \quad \text{(\textcolor{orange}{Marshallian demand}).} $$ & Same, done for each agent separately. \\
\hline
\textbf{(6)} \emph{Market clearing} & \textcolor{orange}{Embedded:} budget binds, nonneg auto from FOC. \emph{Nothing extra to check.} & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{CE viewpoint (decentralized).}} Aggregate market clearing is \emph{not} a constraint in any agent's problem --- it must be \textcolor{orange}{closed separately}:
$$ \sum_h x_i^{h*}(\hat p,\, \hat p \cdot \omega^h) = \sum_h \omega_i^h \;\;\forall i. $$
These $N$ equations determine the equilibrium price vector $\hat p$. SEE dedicated NOTE.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Note on the Planner viewpoint (centralized).}} for the planner aggregate feasibility is \textcolor{orange}{embedded as a constraint from Step 1}, so it need not be checked separately. \\
\end{tabular}



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Footnotes on MRS interpretation.}}

$(\dagger)$ \emph{Internal exchange rate.} At what rate is the consumer willing to exchange $x_2$ for $x_1$? If $\text{MRS} = 4/2 = 2$, then $MU_{x_1}$ is twice $MU_{x_2}$, so the consumer is willing to give up \textbf{2 units of $x_2$ for 1 unit of $x_1$} $=$ \textcolor{orange}{internal price ratio}.

$(\ddagger)$ \emph{Slope of indifference curve.} Along $\{U = \bar U\}$: $dU = 0 \Rightarrow MU_{x_1}\, dx_1 + MU_{x_2}\, dx_2 = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dx_2}{dx_1} = -\dfrac{MU_{x_1}}{MU_{x_2}} = -\text{MRS}.$



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Dynamics --- trade drives convergence (concrete numerical example).}}

\emph{Setup.} Consumer has $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2$: internally willing to give up \textcolor{blue}{$2$ units of $A$ for $1$ unit of $B$}. Market price: \textcolor{blue}{$1$ unit of $B$ costs $2.1$ units of $A$}, i.e.\ $p_b/p_a = 2.1$.

\textbf{Step 1 (compare).} $\;\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2 \;<\; p_b/p_a = 2.1$. Market charges \textcolor{orange}{more for $B$} than consumer values it $\Rightarrow$ $B$ is \emph{overpriced} for this consumer.

\textbf{Step 2 (trade).} Consumer \textcolor{orange}{sells $B$, buys $A$}: pay $1$ unit of $B$, receive $2.1$ units of $A$ (better than internal rate of $2$).

\textbf{Step 3 (concavity of $U$ kicks in).}
$\bullet$ Less $B$ $\;\Rightarrow\; MU_B \uparrow$ (diminishing returns; see Plot 2).
$\bullet$ More $A$ $\;\Rightarrow\; MU_A \downarrow$.
$\bullet$ Hence $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = MU_B/MU_A$ \emph{rises} toward $p_b/p_a = 2.1$.

\textbf{Step 4 (stop at tangency).} When $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2.1$: now to give up $1$ unit of $B$ the consumer demands $2.1$ units of $A$ in compensation --- exactly what the market pays. \emph{No further profitable trade $\Rightarrow$ optimum reached.}

nodes.title: Application: Homothetic Preferences
Application: Quasilinear Preferences
THE MARKET CLEARING DYNAMIC:
nodes.content:
THE MARKET CLEARING DYNAMIC:
- Agents take prices as given, still agent preferences build prices: there is an auctioner proposing some prices, agents are giving their optimal quantities for the given prices, the prices that "work" are those for which agents maximize and markets clear. The prices are then pinned down by **market clearing** where each x is the marshallian demand of a given agent! 
- Aggregate $\omega_a/\omega_b$ does NOT enter Marshallian demand as a function. It enters CE only through the \textbf{market-clearing equation}, which is what pins down prices. After prices are solved, plugging them back into Marshallian demand gives the actual quantities. Ceteris parisbus agrgeagte scarcity of an endowmnt will bring out the relative price of that good.



{{img:0|w=1100}}


Note how the given p gives you a specific demand point. 


high endowments ceteris paribus reduce prices because they reflect a decresing marginal utility

nodes.title: no universal ratio under heterogeneous preferneces
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{This is to make you understand the commonr ation result deries from 1) homothetic prefercnes and 2) homogeneity of such}}

If agents have het. hom. preferences they will demand different opt. consumption ratios. And representative agent assumpt breaks down because agggreagate demand dpends on distirbution of endowmentsgDO NOT

\emph{Common setup:} $\omega^1 = (5, 1),\, \omega^2 = (1, 4),\, \omega = (6, 5)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Setting + Lagrangian (both columns, same form).}} \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} BC binds for sure (monotonicity, $\lambda^h>0$); $x\ge0$ slack for sure (Inada, interior homothetic preferences) --- nothing to test. \emph{Objective:} $\max_{x_a^h,x_b^h}\, U^h(x_a^h,x_b^h)$. \emph{Choice variables:} $x_a^h,x_b^h$. \emph{Constraint (multiplier):} $p_a x_a^h + p_b x_b^h = w^h$ $(\lambda^h)$, with $w^h = p_a\omega_a^h + p_b\omega_b^h$. \emph{Lagrangian:} $\mathcal{L}^h = U^h(x_a^h,x_b^h) - \lambda^h\bigl(p_a x_a^h + p_b x_b^h - w^h\bigr)$; the Step-(2) FOCs are $\partial\mathcal{L}^h/\partial x_a^h=0$ and $\partial\mathcal{L}^h/\partial x_b^h=0$.

\begin{tabular}{p{4cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}}
 & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Col 2: IDENTICAL homothetic}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Col 3: HETEROGENEOUS homothetic}} \\
\textit{Preferences} & both $U^h = x_a^{0.4} x_b^{0.6}$ & $U^1 = x_a^{0.2} x_b^{0.8}$, $\;U^2 = x_a^{0.8} x_b^{0.2}$ \\
\textit{Each agent homothetic?} & \textcolor{green}{✓} & \textcolor{green}{✓} \\
\textit{Same $r^*(p)$ across agents?} & \textcolor{green}{✓} & \textcolor{red}{✗} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1) Agent $h$'s problem.}
$\max U^h$ s.t.\ $p_a x_a + p_b x_b = w^h$, where $w^h = p_a \omega_a^h + p_b \omega_b^h$. &
\emph{Identical Marshallian structure in both columns;} &
\emph{the difference is only in $U^h$ (see row above).} \\
\hline
\textbf{(2) FOCs} (one per good) &
$0.4\, x_a^{-0.6} x_b^{0.6} = \lambda^h p_a$
$0.6\, x_a^{0.4} x_b^{-0.4} = \lambda^h p_b$
\emph{(same form for both agents)} &
Agent 1 ($\alpha = 0.2$): $0.2 \,x_a^{-0.8} x_b^{0.8} = \lambda^1 p_a$, $\,0.8\, x_a^{0.2} x_b^{-0.2} = \lambda^1 p_b$.
Agent 2 ($\alpha = 0.8$): $0.8\, x_a^{-0.2} x_b^{0.2} = \lambda^2 p_a$, $\,0.2\, x_a^{0.8} x_b^{-0.8} = \lambda^2 p_b$. \\
\hline
\textbf{(3) Ratio of FOCs} (kill $\lambda^h$) $\to$ $r^*(p)$ &
$\dfrac{x_a^h}{x_b^h} = \dfrac{0.4}{0.6}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = \dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r^*(p).$
\textcolor{orange}{Same function for both agents.} &
Agent 1: $\dfrac{x_a^1}{x_b^1} = \dfrac{0.2}{0.8}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = \dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r_1^*(p).$
Agent 2: $\dfrac{x_a^2}{x_b^2} = \dfrac{0.8}{0.2}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = 4\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r_2^*(p).$
\textcolor{red}{Different functions: $r_1^* \neq r_2^*$.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(4) FOC ratio $+$ budget} $\to$ \emph{Marshallian demand}.
Take budget $p_a x_a^h + p_b x_b^h = w^h$ (with $w^h = p_a \omega_a^h + p_b \omega_b^h$ known), and plug in $p_b/p_a$ from the FOC ratio (Step 3) to eliminate one variable. &
$r^*(p) = \tfrac{2}{3}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$.
$p_a r^* + p_b = \tfrac{2}{3} p_b + p_b = \tfrac{5}{3} p_b.$
$x_b^h \cdot \tfrac{5}{3} p_b = w^h \;\Rightarrow\; x_b^h = \tfrac{3}{5}\dfrac{w^h}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.6\, w^h}{p_b}.$
$x_a^h = r^*(p)\, x_b^h = \tfrac{2}{3}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a} \cdot \tfrac{3}{5}\tfrac{w^h}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.4\, w^h}{p_a}.$
\textcolor{orange}{Same coefficient $0.4$ on $w^h$ for both agents.} &
\emph{Agent 1} ($r_1^* = \tfrac{1}{4}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$): $p_a r_1^* + p_b = \tfrac{1}{4} p_b + p_b = \tfrac{5}{4} p_b.$
$x_b^1 = \tfrac{4}{5}\dfrac{w^1}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.8\, w^1}{p_b}.\;\;x_a^1 = r_1^* x_b^1 = \dfrac{0.2\, w^1}{p_a}.$
\emph{Agent 2} ($r_2^* = 4\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$): $p_a r_2^* + p_b = 4 p_b + p_b = 5 p_b.$
$x_b^2 = \tfrac{1}{5}\dfrac{w^2}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.2\, w^2}{p_b}.\;\;x_a^2 = r_2^* x_b^2 = \dfrac{0.8\, w^2}{p_a}.$
\textcolor{red}{Different coefficients on $w^h$ across agents.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(5) Market clearing for $A$} \emph{(the pivot step)} &
$\sum_h x_a^h = \dfrac{0.4 (w^1 + w^2)}{p_a} = \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.4\,(p_a \omega_a + p_b \omega_b) = p_a \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.4(6 p_a + 5 p_b) = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 2 p_b = 3.6 p_a.$
 &
$\sum_h x_a^h = \dfrac{0.2\, w^1 + 0.8\, w^2}{p_a} = \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.2(5 p_a + p_b) + 0.8(p_a + 4 p_b) = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 1.8 p_a + 3.4 p_b = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 3.4 p_b = 4.2 p_a.$
 \\
\hline
\textbf{(6) Equilibrium prices} &
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 3.6/2 = 1.8.$
\emph{Normalize:} $\hat p_a = 1$, $\hat p_b = 1.8.$ &
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 4.2/3.4 \approx 1.235.$
\emph{Normalize:} $\hat p_a = 1$, $\hat p_b \approx 1.235.$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(7) Wealths at CE} &
$w^1 = 5 + 1.8 = 6.8$, $w^2 = 1 + 7.2 = 8.2$. &
$w^1 = 5 + 1.235 = 6.235$, $w^2 = 1 + 4.94 = 5.94$. \\
\hline
\textbf{(8) Individual demands and ratios} &
$x^1 = (0.4 \cdot 6.8,\, 0.6 \cdot 6.8 / 1.8) = (2.72,\, 2.267)$.
$x^2 = (3.28,\, 2.733)$.
\emph{Ratios:} $2.72/2.267 = 1.2$;\; $3.28/2.733 = 1.2$.
\textcolor{orange}{Both $= \omega_a/\omega_b = 1.2$.} &
$x^1 \approx (0.2 \cdot 6.235,\; 0.8 \cdot 6.235 / 1.235) \approx (1.247,\, 4.039)$.
$x^2 \approx (4.752,\, 0.962)$.
\emph{Ratios:} $1.247/4.039 \approx 0.31$;\; $4.752/0.962 \approx 4.94$.
\textcolor{red}{Wildly different; neither $= 1.2$.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(*) Swap test} \;($\omega^1 \leftrightarrow \omega^2$, same aggregate) &
Identical agents $\Rightarrow$ swapping is a relabel: clearing equation \emph{unchanged}.
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 1.8$ (\textcolor{green}{unchanged}).
\textcolor{orange}{Distribution irrelevant.} &
After swap: $0.2(p_a + 4 p_b) + 0.8(5 p_a + p_b) = 6 p_a \Rightarrow 4.2 p_a + 1.6 p_b = 6 p_a \Rightarrow \hat p_b/\hat p_a = 1.125$.
\textcolor{red}{Prices change from $1.235$ to $1.125$.}
Distribution \textcolor{red}{matters}. \\
\end{tabular}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Verification.}} Interior regime confirmed: demands strictly positive (Inada) and budgets hold with equality --- no regime switch needed.

nodes.title: Representative Agent Assumption
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{REPRESENTATIVE AGENT --- when can one agent stand in for the whole population?}}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{1. What is the problem we are trying to solve?}}

Suppose there are $H$ consumers. Consumer $h$ has wealth $w^h$, preferences $U^h$, and therefore demand
$$ x_i^{h*}(p, w^h; U^h). $$
If we want total demand for good $i$, normally we have to solve every consumer's problem and add them:
$$ X_i = \sum_h x_i^{h*}(p, w^h; U^h). $$
A representative agent allows us to avoid doing this. We ask whether there exists \emph{one} hypothetical consumer, with preferences $U^R$ and total wealth $W=\sum_h w^h$, whose demand is exactly aggregate demand:
$$ \boxed{\;\sum_h x_i^{h*}(p, w^h; U^h) = x_i^{R*}(p, W; U^R)\quad \forall i.\;} $$
\emph{So instead of solving $H$ optimization problems, we solve one.} CRUCIALLY, you need Demand not to depend on wealth W or utility shape U (you need identical homothetic preferences)!





\bigskip
\textbf{Two canonical families that satisfy Gorman aggregation:}

\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{1. Homothetic preferences}} --- whatever the wealth, agents all consume the same RATIO.

\textbf{So think about the optimization:} there is a given aggregate $\omega_a/\omega_b$ ratio, and in the identical-homothetic case all agents pick the \emph{same} individual consumption ratio $x_a^h/x_b^h$ (because they share the same homothetic preferences, so ratios are wealth-independent and identical across agents). The aggregate consumption ratio --- being a sum of identical individual ratios --- equals that common individual ratio. Market clearing then forces it to equal $\omega_a/\omega_b$.

\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{2. Quasilinear preferences}} --- whatever the endowment, agents all consume the same NON-NUMERAIRE $y$.

nodes.title: Elasticities on the Marshallian demands
Application: Labor Supply Elasticities (General, Frisch, Applied)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{LABOR SUPPLY ELASTICITIES --- general, Frisch, applied:}}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{1. Setting.}} \emph{Objective:} $\max_{c,h}\,U(c)-v(h)$; \emph{choice variables} $c,h>0$; \emph{constraint} $c = wh + I$ $(\lambda)$. ($U$ concave in $c$, $v$ convex in $h$.)
\[ \max_{c, h} \;U(c) - v(h) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad c = w h + I, \;\; c, h > 0. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{2. Lagrangian.}} (multiplier $\lambda$ on the budget)
\[ \mathcal{L} = U(c) - v(h) - \lambda\,(c - w h - I). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Question.}} How does the optimal hours $h^*$ respond to a wage change?
\[ \boxed{\;\epsilon_{h, w} \;:=\; \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} \cdot \dfrac{w}{h^*}.\;} \]



\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Reminder: every FOC step starts by setting the relevant partial of $\mathcal{L}$ to $0$.}}

\textbf{Notation:} the multiplier $\lambda^*$ depends on the \emph{exogenous} parameters of the Lagrangian $(w, I)$ --- never on the endogenous choice variables $c, h$ (they get absorbed into $c^*(w, I), h^*(w, I)$ after solving).

\begin{tabular}{p{7cm}|p{13cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}}
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{GENERAL}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{FRISCH ($\bar\lambda$ fixed)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{APPLIED}  $v(h) = h^{1+1/\epsilon}/(1+1/\epsilon)$, $U(c) = c$} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1) Retrieve $h^*$} from FOC w.r.t.\ $h$. &
\textbf{FOC$_h$:} $-v'(h^*) + \lambda^*(w, I)\, w = 0$
$\Rightarrow v'(h^*(w, I)) = w \lambda^*(w, I)$

A wage change has two channels:

$\bullet$ \textcolor{blue}{Direct ($+\Delta w$):} higher wage $\to$ more work.
$\bullet$ \textcolor{blue}{Indirect / income ($-\Delta w$):} $\lambda^* \downarrow$ (richer $\to$ less marginal value of $c$) $\to$ work less. &
\textbf{FOC$_h$:} $-v'(h^*) + \bar\lambda\, w = 0$
$\Rightarrow v'(h^*) = w \bar\lambda$

\emph{(no income effect: $\bar\lambda$ fixed by assumption $\Rightarrow$ only the direct channel survives)} &
\textbf{FOC$_h$:} $-h^{*\,1/\epsilon} + \bar\lambda\, w = 0$
$\Rightarrow h^*(w, \lambda) = (w \lambda)^{\epsilon}$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(2) Find $\lambda^*$} from FOC w.r.t.\ $c$. &
\textbf{FOC$_c$:} $U'(c^*) - \lambda^* = 0$
$\Rightarrow \lambda^*(w, I) = U'(c^*(w, I))$
\emph{(depends on $w, I$ through $c^*$)} &
\emph{No need;} $\bar\lambda$ fixed by assumption. &
\textbf{FOC$_c$:} $1 - \lambda^* = 0$
\emph{(since $U(c) = c \Rightarrow U'(c) = 1$)}
$\Rightarrow \lambda^* = \bar\lambda = 1$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(3) Compute $\partial h^*/\partial w$.} Differentiate FOC$_h$ (and FOC$_c$, FOC$_{BC}$ where needed) w.r.t.\ $w$. &
From FOC$_h$ (product rule): $v''(h^*)\, \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} = \lambda^*(w, I) + w\, \boxed{\dfrac{\partial \lambda^*}{\partial w}}$

\emph{Need} $\boxed{\partial \lambda^*/\partial w}$. From FOC$_c$ (chain rule): $\boxed{\dfrac{\partial \lambda^*}{\partial w}} = U''(c^*)\, \boxed{\dfrac{\partial c^*}{\partial w}}$

\emph{Need} $\boxed{\partial c^*/\partial w}$. From FOC$_{BC}$ (product rule): $\boxed{\dfrac{\partial c^*}{\partial w}} = h^* + w\, \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w}$
 &
From FOC$_h$ (with $\partial \bar\lambda/\partial w = 0$):
$v''(h^*)\, \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} = \bar\lambda$ &
Direct from $h^*(w, \bar\lambda) = (w\bar\lambda)^{\epsilon}$:
$\dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} = \epsilon\, \bar\lambda^{\epsilon}\, w^{\epsilon - 1}$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(4) Convert to elasticity:} multiply by $w/h^*$. &
Substitute (FOC$_c$, FOC$_{BC}$) into the differentiated FOC$_h$ and solve:
$\boxed{\;\epsilon_{h, w} = -\dfrac{U'(c^*) + h^* w\, U''(c^*)}{w^2 U''(c^*) - v''(h^*)} \cdot \dfrac{w}{h^*}\;}$ &
$\epsilon^{F}_{h, w} = \dfrac{\underbrace{\bar\lambda\, w}_{v'(h^*)}}{v''(h^*)\, h^*}$
 &
$\epsilon^{*}_{h, w} = \epsilon\, \bar\lambda^{\epsilon} w^{\epsilon - 1} \cdot \dfrac{w}{(w \bar\lambda)^{\epsilon}}$
$\Rightarrow \boxed{\;\epsilon^{*}_{h, w} = \epsilon\;}$ \\
\end{tabular}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{LABOR SUPPLY ELASTICITIES WITH TAXES --- general, Frisch, applied:}}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{1. Setting (with labor income tax).}} \emph{Objective:} $\max_{c,h}\,U(c)-v(h)$; \emph{choice variables} $c,h>0$; \emph{constraint} $c=(1-\tau)wh+I$ $(\lambda)$.
\[
\max_{c,h} \; U(c)-v(h)
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad
c=(1-\tau)wh+I, \qquad c,h>0.
\]

Here \(\tau\) is the proportional labor income tax and \(1-\tau\) is the net-of-tax rate. The gross wage is \(w\), while the private net wage is \((1-\tau)w\).

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{2. Lagrangian.}}
\[
\mathcal{L}
=
U(c)-v(h)-\lambda\big(c-(1-\tau)wh-I\big).
\]

now optimal h* will depend on $\tau$ as well!

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{3. FOCs.}}
\[ \text{FOC}_c:\ U'(c^*)-\lambda^*=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda^*=U'(c^*), \qquad \text{FOC}_h:\ -v'(h^*)+\lambda^*(1-\tau)w=0. \]
\[ \boxed{\ v'(h^*)=(1-\tau)\,w\,U'(c^*).\ } \]
\emph{Identical to the no-tax FOC with the wage replaced by the \textbf{net wage} $(1-\tau)w$}, so every elasticity carries over under $w\mapsto(1-\tau)w$ (e.g.\ $\varepsilon_{h,1-\tau}$ mirrors $\varepsilon_{h,w}$).
\textbf{Applied} ($U(c)=c$, $v(h)=h^{1+1/\varepsilon}/(1+1/\varepsilon)$): $\lambda^*=1$ and $h^{*\,1/\varepsilon}=(1-\tau)w \Rightarrow \boxed{\,h^*=\big((1-\tau)w\big)^{\varepsilon}\,}$, giving net-of-tax elasticity $\varepsilon_{h,1-\tau}=\varepsilon$ (the higher the tax, the lower hours, with elasticity $\varepsilon$).

Exchange Economy — setting and feasibility
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXCHANGE ECONOMY --- the standard setting for PO and CE.}}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Ingredients.}}
$\bullet$ \textbf{$I$ consumers / agents}, indexed by $i = 1, 2, \ldots, I$.
$\bullet$ \textbf{$N$ goods}, indexed by $n = 1, 2, \ldots, N$.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Initial endowments} $\omega^i = (\omega_1^i, \ldots, \omega_N^i) \in \mathbb{R}^N_+$: agent $i$'s initial stock of each good \emph{before} any trade.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Utility functions} $U^i : \mathbb{R}^N_+ \to \mathbb{R}$, one per agent.
$\bullet$ **GE setting**: 
- Anonymous agents interacitng, they are small, they take prices as given
- General equilibrium: all prices are free to adjust vs Partial Equilirbium, some prices are fixed
$\bullet$ **No production **--- the only way goods change hands is by exchange between consumers.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Feasible set.}}
$$ \mathcal{F} \;=\; \bigl\{\, x = (x^1, \ldots, x^I) \;:\; x_n^i \geq 0 \;\forall i, n, \;\; \textstyle\sum_i x_n^i = \omega_n \;\forall n \,\bigr\}. $$

Remark: **price takers** agents mean they do not know they cannot affect prices. But then note that at CE we look for prices such that AS = AD, and this clearly is composed of individual agents demand decisions!

nodes.title: PO and CE: FWT and SWT
nodes.content:
If CE exists (given this omega), is it PO? 

YES \textbf{\textcolor{red}{FIRST WELFARE THEOREM --- every CE is Pareto Optimal.}}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Statement.}} If $(\hat p, \hat x)$ is a Competitive Equilibrium \emph{and} each $U^i$ is strictly increasing in every good, then $\hat x$ is Pareto Optimal.
$$ \boxed{\;\text{CE} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \text{PO}\quad \text{(under strict monotonicity)}.\;} $$
Moreover $U^i(\hat x_i) \ge U^i(\omega^i)$
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof sketch.}}
\textbf{(i)} Suppose for contradiction $\hat x$ is not PO. Then $\exists y \in \mathcal{F}$ with $U^i(y^i) \geq U^i(\hat x^i)$ $\forall i$ (ahemts) and strict for some $j$.
\textbf{(ii)} Strict monotonicity $+$ consumer optimization at prices $\hat p$:
$\bullet$ For agent $j$ (strictly better off): $\hat p \cdot y^j > \hat p \cdot \hat x^j$ (otherwise $y^j$ would have been chosen). The point is that he is already at the boudnary and this $y^j$ is not feasible
$\bullet$ For other agents: $\hat p \cdot y^i \geq \hat p \cdot \hat x^i$.
\textbf{(iii)} Sum: $\hat p \cdot \sum_i y^i \;>\; \hat p \cdot \sum_i \hat x^i = \omega$. Not feasible!

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Key takeaway.}} CE allocations are always on the \emph{*Pareto Set*} (and in fact on the \emph{Contract Curve}, since they're individually rational by construction). The market efficiently rules out wasteful allocations \emph{without a planner}.

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{What FWT does NOT say.}}
$\bullet$ CE allocations need not be \emph{fair}. The endowment distribution determines who gets what at the CE.



If a point is PO, can some $\omega$ exists where $\hat x$ is the CE ? failure is not CE non existence for one omega, but for all omega.
\bigskip
\bigskip





 \textbf{\textcolor{red}{SECOND WELFARE THEOREM --- any PO can be supported as a CE with lump-sum transfers.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Statement (ALL CASES EXCEPT THE ONES UNDER "CE FAILURE").}} Under \emph{convexity of preferences} (concave $U^i$), \emph{strict monotonicity}, and continuity: \emph{any} Pareto-optimal allocation $\bar x$ can be supported as a CE relative to some prices $\hat p \in \mathbb{R}^N_+$ \emph{after} lump-sum transfers $T = (T^1, \ldots, T^I)$ with $\sum_i T^i = 0$.

$$ \boxed{\;\text{Any PO} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \text{CE} \;\;\text{with transfers (under convexity)}.\;} $$
Basically under such assumptions always exists prices that support a given PO equilibrium





\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this matters.}}
$\bullet$ \textcolor{orange}{Equity-efficiency separation.} The planner can pick the most equitable PO and \emph{implement it via the price mechanism} just by redistributing endowments. Market efficiency and distributional choice are separable.
$\bullet$ \textcolor{orange}{Decentralization.} A planner doesn't need to choose individual allocations --- they just set transfers and let markets clear.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Super-concise intuition:}}
We are saying that the PO allocation can be decentralized through a market and through prices

Recall PO allocation is characterized by this efficiency condition (assuming interior, differentiable solution ): 
$$ \frac{\partial U^i/\partial x^i_n}{\partial U^i/\partial x^i_m} \;=\; \frac{\mu_n}{\mu_m} \qquad \text{for both } i=1, 2. $$
\emph{Each agent's MRS equals the planner's relative shadow prices.} That is, the marginal value of consuming one extra unit of good l and the marginal value of consuming the extra unit of good h. What is this?? exacly the same role of prices in the CE

To implement the PO as a CE, it is enough then to use a system of prices
$$ \frac{\partial U^i/\partial x^i_n}{\partial U^i/\partial x^i_m} \;=\; \frac{p_n}{p_m}. $$
\emph{Same equations, with $p$ replacing $\mu$.}

\emph{The link.} Set $\;\boxed{\;p_n \,=\, \mu_n\;}\;$ (up to a positive normalization). Then the planner's allocation \emph{is} a consumer-optimal bundle at those prices --- the FOCs match. 


How do you change prices? 
Lump-sum transfers $T^i$ are picked so each agent's budget at $p$ exactly affords the planner's bundle: $p \cdot \bar x^i = p \cdot \omega^i + T^i$, with $\sum_i T^i = 0$.

\textbf{Slogan:} \emph{decentralization is just renaming Lagrange multipliers as prices}. The planner's shadow prices on market clearing $=$ the CE market prices.

nodes.title: Optimal Linear Taxation --- 1st Best vs 2nd Best
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{OPTIMAL LINEAR TAXATION.}}

You are in the leisure / hours of work decision framework. 

- in this model inequality is generated by $\omega$ (skill) distribution <- role of endowment
- some people may have a lot of  $\omega$  and hence consume a lot, some people little and consume little
- The first wefare theorem says nothig about distribution. This situation is efficient -> the gov may wish to distribute:
     - 2nd WT says that with lump sum transfers the planer can control each ppl consumption and hours of work. So, if the governmetn can observe each person $\omega_i$ it can, a priori, tax people on skill. This tax is totally unrealated to how much you work, whether you work or not you are taxed the same, so you end up working as much as before this tax. The planner choice var is B (lump sum transfers, a priori) and can allow him to distirbute as he wishes on the first best 
     -  the issue is that $\omega_i$ is not observable. what you observe about people is $y_i = \omega_i * h_i$. You cannot act a priori with lump sum. You see how much they produce and you rax their prdocution. But if before they were producing at $MB_h = MC_h$ now $MB_h^t < MC_h$ they react endogenously to the planner move! => efficiency loss! Explained: Before taxation, individuals choose hours of work such that \(MB_h^{\text{priv = social}} = MC_h^{\text{priv = social}\), implying an efficient allocation. Suppose now that the government levies a tax on labor income. The worker no longer receives the full marginal benefit generated by an additional hour of work, but only the after-tax return. The labor supply condition becomes \(MB_h^{\text{private}} = (1-\tau)MB_h^{\text{social}} = MC_h\).As a result, there may exist hours of work for which \(MB_h^{\text{social}} > MC_h\), while \(MB_h^{\text{private}} \leq MC_h\). For instance, the social marginal benefit of an additional hour may be \(11\), while the marginal cost is \(10\). Without taxation, the individual would work that hour because \(11 > 10\). However, if a tax reduces the worker's return by \(1\), then \(MB_h^{\text{private}} = 10 = MC_h\). The worker is no longer willing to supply that additional hour even though its social value exceeds its social cost. The tax therefore creates a wedge between the social and private returns to work. As a consequence, some hours satisfying \(MB_h^{\text{social}} > MC_h\) are no longer supplied, generating a distortion in labor supply and an associated efficiency loss (deadweight loss).

Note: if lambda bar is fixed we have no income effect of taxation. otherwise we have
- standard distencentive to work  int he work foc
- tax -> less consumption- > higher lambda ->  indirect incentive to work in the lambda foc!

nodes.title: Guiding example --- worker + planner, utilitarian and Rawlsian
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{GUIDING EXAMPLE --- worker + planner, two parametrisations.}}

\emph{Population: a $\%$ of skills $w_i$ with frequencies $\pi_i$. Planner balances $\sum_i \pi_i T(y_i) = G = 0$.}

\begin{tabular}{p{7cm}|p{15.5cm}|p{15.5cm}}
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Example 1 --- linear tax, quasi-linear $U$}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Example 2 --- HSV schedule, log $U$}} \\
\hline
\textbf{0. Setting.} \emph{Utility and tax schedule.} & $U(c, h) = c - \dfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma}$, $\gamma > 0$.

$T(y) = -B + \tau y$,\;\; $y = w h$,\;\; $c = B + (1-\tau)\, w\, h$.

\emph{Linear flat tax.} & $U(c, h) = \ln c - \dfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma}$.

$T(y) = y - B y^{1-\tau}$,\;\; $c = B\, y^{1-\tau}$.

\emph{Sub} $y = w h$:\;\; $c = B\,(w h)^{1-\tau}$.

\emph{Multiplicative HSV.} \\
\hline
\textbf{Govt budget.} $G = 0 \Rightarrow \sum_i \pi_i T(y_i) = 0$ & $\sum_i \pi_i \tau y_i = B$

$\Rightarrow\; B = \tau\, Y(\tau)$,\;\; $Y(\tau) = \sum_i \pi_i\, w_i\, h^*(\tau, w_i)$. & $\sum_i \pi_i B y_i^{1-\tau} = \sum_i \pi_i y_i = Y(\tau)$,\;\; with $Y(\tau) = \sum_i \pi_i\, w_i\, h^*(\tau, w_i)$.

$\Rightarrow\; B(\tau) = \dfrac{Y(\tau)}{\sum_i \pi_i\, y_i^{1-\tau}} = \dfrac{\sum_i \pi_i\, w_i\, h^*(\tau, w_i)}{\sum_i \pi_i\, \bigl(w_i\, h^*(\tau, w_i)\bigr)^{1-\tau}}$. \\
\hline
\textbf{① Worker picks $h^*$.} \emph{Setting:} objective $U(c,h)$, choice $h$, constraint $c=y-T(y)$ $(\lambda)$. \emph{The budget is an equality $\Rightarrow$ substitute it into $U$ (equivalently $\lambda=U_c$), leaving an unconstrained max in $h$; the FOC below is $\partial U/\partial h=0$.} \emph{($B$ taken as given!)} & $\displaystyle h^* = \arg\max_{h \geq 0}\; \bigl[\, c - \tfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \,\bigr]\;\;\text{sub.}\;\; c = y - T(y)$.

\emph{Expand $T(y)$:} $c = y - (-B + \tau y) = B + (1-\tau)\, y$.

\emph{Expand $y = w h$:} $c = B + (1-\tau)\, w\, h$.

$\Rightarrow\; \max_{h \geq 0}\; \bigl[ B + (1-\tau)\, w\, h - \tfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \bigr]$.

\textbf{FOC:} $(1-\tau)\, w = h^\gamma$.

$\boxed{\; h^*(\tau, w) = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma}\, w^{1/\gamma},\;\; \varepsilon = 1/\gamma. \;}$ & $\displaystyle h^* = \arg\max_{h \geq 0}\; \bigl[\, \ln c - \tfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \,\bigr]\;\;\text{sub.}\;\; c = y - T(y)$.

\emph{Expand $T(y)$:} $c = y - (y - B y^{1-\tau}) = B\, y^{1-\tau}$.

\emph{Expand $y = w h$:} $c = B\,(w h)^{1-\tau}\;\Rightarrow\; \ln c = \ln B + (1-\tau)(\ln w + \ln h)$.

$\Rightarrow\; \max_{h \geq 0}\; \bigl[ \ln B + (1-\tau)(\ln w + \ln h) - \tfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \bigr]$.

\textbf{FOC:} $(1-\tau)/h = h^\gamma$.

$\boxed{\; h^*(\tau) = (1-\tau)^{1/(1+\gamma)}. \;}$

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Doesn't depend on $w$ $\to$ no effect on his workload!}} \\
\hline
\textbf{② Planner picks $\tau$ --- 2A) Utilitarian.} \emph{Setting:} objective $W^U=\sum_i\pi_i U_i$, choice $\tau$, constraint $\sum_i\pi_i T(y_i)=0$ $(\eta)$. \emph{Govt budget substituted via $B=\tau Y(\tau)$ $\Rightarrow$ unconstrained max in $\tau$; FOC $\partial W^U/\partial\tau=0$.} \emph{Knowing worker's $h^*(\tau,w)$ response.}& \textbf{1.} Write $W^U = \sum_i \pi_i \bigl[ c_i - \tfrac{h_i^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \bigr]$.

\textbf{2.} Sub $c_i = B + (1-\tau)\, w_i\, h_i$:

$W^U = B + \sum_i \pi_i \bigl[ (1-\tau)\, w_i\, h_i - \tfrac{h_i^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \bigr]$.

\textbf{3.} Sub $h_i^* = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma} w_i^{1/\gamma}$. Both terms become $(1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma}\, w_i^{1+1/\gamma}$:

$W^U = B + (1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma}\!\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1+1/\gamma} - \tfrac{(1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma}}{1+\gamma}\!\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1+1/\gamma}$.

\textbf{4.} Call $M := \sum_i \pi_i\, w_i^{1+1/\gamma}$:

$W^U = B + (1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma} M - \tfrac{(1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma}}{1+\gamma}\, M$.

\textbf{5.} Sub $B = \tau\, Y_t$. With $y_i = w_i h_i^* = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma} w_i^{1+1/\gamma}$, $Y_t = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma} M$:

$B = \tau\,(1-\tau)^{1/\gamma}\, M\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;$
$W^U(\tau) = \tau\,(1-\tau)^{1/\gamma} M + (1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma} M - \tfrac{(1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma}}{1+\gamma}\, M$.

\textbf{6.} Expand the central term: $(1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma} = (1-\tau)\cdot(1-\tau)^{1/\gamma}$:

$W^U(\tau) = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma} M \bigl[\, \tau + (1-\tau) - \tfrac{1-\tau}{1+\gamma} \,\bigr]$.

\textbf{7.} Factor: $\tau + (1-\tau) = 1$, so

$\boxed{\;\; W^U(\tau) = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma}\, M\, \Bigl[\, 1 - \dfrac{1-\tau}{1+\gamma} \,\Bigr]\,. \;\;}$ & \textbf{1.} Write $W^U = \sum_i \pi_i\bigl[ \ln c_i - \tfrac{h_i^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma}\bigr]$.

\textbf{2.} Sub $c_i = B\, y_i^{1-\tau}$:

$W^U = \ln B + (1-\tau)\sum_i \pi_i \ln y_i - \sum_i \pi_i \tfrac{h_i^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma}$.

\textbf{3.} Sub $h_i^* = (1-\tau)^{1/(1+\gamma)}$, $y_i = w_i\,(1-\tau)^{1/(1+\gamma)}$, so $h_i^{1+\gamma} = 1-\tau$:

$W^U = \ln B + (1-\tau)\sum_i \pi_i \ln w_i + \tfrac{1-\tau}{1+\gamma}\ln(1-\tau) - \tfrac{1-\tau}{1+\gamma}$.

\textbf{4.} \emph{(No $M$ aggregator needed --- the labor terms are not $w$-weighted because $h^*$ is independent of $w$.)}

\textbf{5.} Sub $B(\tau) = (1-\tau)^{\tau/(1+\gamma)} \cdot \dfrac{\sum_i \pi_i w_i}{\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}}$:

$\ln B(\tau) = \tfrac{\tau}{1+\gamma}\ln(1-\tau) + \ln\!\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i\bigr) - \ln\!\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}\bigr)$.

\textbf{6--7.} Combine ($\tau + (1-\tau) = 1$ collapses the $\ln(1-\tau)$ terms):

$\boxed{\;\; W^U(\tau) = \dfrac{1}{1+\gamma}\bigl[\ln(1-\tau) - (1-\tau)\bigr] + (1-\tau)\sum_i \pi_i \ln w_i + \ln\!\Bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i\Bigr) - \ln\!\Bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}\Bigr). \;\;}$

\emph{Closed form --- but only the FOC blows up.} \\
\hline
\textbf{FOC} $\partial W^U / \partial \tau = 0$. & \emph{Trick: let $T := 1-\tau$, so $dT/d\tau = -1$. The FOC in $\tau$ becomes the FOC in $T$, just sign-flipped.}

Rewrite $W^U = T^{1/\gamma}\, M\,\dfrac{1+\gamma - T}{1+\gamma}$ (since $1 - T/(1+\gamma) = (1+\gamma - T)/(1+\gamma)$).

$\dfrac{\partial W^U}{\partial T} = \dfrac{M}{1+\gamma}\Bigl[\tfrac{1}{\gamma}T^{1/\gamma - 1}(1+\gamma - T) - T^{1/\gamma}\Bigr] = \dfrac{M\, T^{1/\gamma - 1}}{\gamma}\,(1 - T) = 0$.

$\Rightarrow\; T = 1\;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\;\; \tau^{*\,U} = 0. \;\;}$

\textcolor{orange}{\emph{QL utility $\Rightarrow$ planner has \textbf{no taste for redistribution} (linear in $c$); only efficiency matters --- optimum is laissez-faire.}} & Differentiate the boxed $W^U(\tau)$ above. The term $-\ln\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}\bigr)$ has derivative

$\dfrac{\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau} \ln w_i}{\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}} \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{1-\tau}[\ln w]$

--- a $\tau$-dependent weighted log-moment of the skill distribution.

FOC: $-\dfrac{1}{(1+\gamma)(1-\tau)} - \dfrac{1}{1+\gamma} - \sum_i \pi_i \ln w_i + \mathbb{E}_{1-\tau}[\ln w] = 0$.

\textcolor{red}{\emph{Transcendental in $\tau$ --- closed-form $W^U$ exists but FOC needs a numerical $\tau^{*\,U}$.}} \\
\hline
\textbf{2B) Rawlsian.} \emph{Max utility of the worst-off agent.} & Assume $w_1 = 0 \Rightarrow h_1^* = 0$, $y_1 = 0$, $c_1 = B$ \emph{(lives off the transfer)}.

$W^R(\tau) = U(c_1, 0) = c_1 = B = \tau\, Y(\tau) = \tau\,(1-\tau)^{1/\gamma}\, M$.

\emph{Trick: $T := 1-\tau$, so $\tau = 1 - T$ and $W^R = (1 - T)\, T^{1/\gamma}\, M$.}

\textbf{FOC:} $\dfrac{\partial W^R}{\partial T} = M\, T^{1/\gamma - 1}\,\dfrac{1 - T(1+\gamma)}{\gamma} = 0$.

$\Rightarrow\; T = \dfrac{1}{1+\gamma}\;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\;\; \tau^{*\,R} = \dfrac{\gamma}{1+\gamma}. \;\;}$

\textcolor{orange}{\emph{Coincides with the Laffer peak --- Rawlsian taxes all the way to revenue max.}} & Same logic: worst-off has $w_1 = 0$, $c_1 = B(\tau)$, $W^R(\tau) = \ln B(\tau)$.

$\ln B(\tau) = \tfrac{\tau}{1+\gamma}\ln(1-\tau) + \ln\!\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i\bigr) - \ln\!\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}\bigr)$.

FOC also mixes $\ln(1-\tau)$ and a $\tau$-dependent weighted average $\Rightarrow$ \textcolor{red}{\emph{numerical $\tau^{*\,R}$.}} \\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Efficiency vs equity --- why the FB shape matters.}}

{{img:0|w=900}}

\textbf{Left} (Example 1, $U(c) = c$ $\Rightarrow$ linear FB). Isowelfare lines $\lambda u_1 + (1-\lambda) u_2 = $ const are \emph{parallel} to the FB. So every point on the FB sits on the \emph{same} isowelfare line $\Rightarrow$ the planner is indifferent among FB allocations $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{no welfare gain from redistribution} $\Rightarrow$ $\tau^{*\,U} = 0$.

\textbf{Right} (Example 2, $U(c) = \ln c$ $\Rightarrow$ concave FB). The FB curve is \emph{steeper than the isowelfare lines} at the rich end and \emph{flatter} at the poor end. A lump-sum transfer from rich (point $A$, the CE projection) to the symmetric point $B$ on the FB lands on a \emph{higher} isowelfare line $\Rightarrow$ $W(B) > W(A)$ $\Rightarrow$ \emph{equity offsets efficiency} $\Rightarrow$ positive $\tau^{*\,U}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-refs:}} setup (1st vs 2nd best UPF), HSV framework (Example 2 tax schedule), Rawlsian + Laffer (deeper dive).

nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXTERNALITIES --- Planner vs CE.}}



\textbf{Def.} Agent $i$ optimises his consumption based \emph{only on his own MU}, \emph{not accounting for spillovers to other agents}.



\begin{tabular}{p{4.3cm}|p{4.3cm}|p{4.3cm}|p{4.3cm}|p{4.3cm}}
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{PLANNER}} NO PROBLEM FOR THE PLANNER & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{CE}} PROBLEM & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{PIGOU TAX}} SOLUTION 1 & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{SUBSIDY}} SOLUTION 2 & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{MISSING MARKET (COASE)}} SOLUTION 3 \\
\hline
\begin{keydef} \fcnum{8a}
\textbf{Problem $P(\bar U)$.}
$$ \max_{y,x}\; U^1(y^1)+x^1 \;\;\text{s.t.} $$
$\bullet$ $y^1+y^2\le\omega_y\ (\mu_y)$ \;[1]
$\bullet$ $x^1+x^2\le\omega_x\ (\mu_x)$ \;[2]
$\bullet$ $U^2(y^2)-\varphi(y^1)+x^2\ge\bar U\ (\lambda)$ \;[3]
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} [1],[2] bind for sure (monotone utilities); [3] binds for sure ($\lambda>0$: otherwise the planner raises $U^1$). Nothing to test.
\end{keydef} & \begin{keydef} \fcnum{8b}
\textbf{Each agent (price-taker),} taking prices and $y^j$ as given:
$$ \textbf{A1:}\ \max_{y^1,x^1}\ U^1(y^1)+x^1 $$
$$ \text{s.t.}\ \ p_1 y^1+x^1=M_1\quad(\lambda_1), $$
$$ \textbf{A2:}\ \max_{y^2,x^2}\ U^2(y^2)-\varphi(y^1)+x^2 $$
$$ \text{s.t.}\ \ p_2 y^2+x^2=M_2\quad(\lambda_2), $$
$M_i:=\omega_x^i+p_1\omega_y^i$.
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} Budgets bind for sure (monotonicity, $\lambda_i>0$); interior regime here --- \textcolor{orange}{corner regimes ($\mu_y=0$, destruction) are TESTED in the worked PLANNER SOLUTION table}.
\end{keydef} & \begin{keydef} \fcnum{8c}
\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{Tax $t$ per unit of $y^1$}; revenue $T=t\,y^1$ rebated lump-sum $T_1,T_2$:}
$$ \boxed{\textcolor{blue}{\,T_1+T_2=T=t\,y^1\ \text{(GOV BC)}\,}} $$
$$ \textbf{A1:}\ \max_{y^1,x^1}\ U^1(y^1)+x^1 $$
$$ \text{s.t.}\ \ (p_1\textcolor{blue}{+t})y^1+x^1=M_1\textcolor{blue}{+T_1}\quad(\lambda_1), $$
$$ \textbf{A2:}\ \max_{y^2,x^2}\ U^2(y^2)-\varphi(y^1)+x^2 $$
$$ \text{s.t.}\ \ p_2 y^2+x^2=M_2\textcolor{blue}{+T_2}\quad(\lambda_2). $$
\end{keydef} & \begin{keydef} \fcnum{8d}
\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{Subsidy $s$ per unit NOT consumed}} vs the pre-policy CE level $\bar y^{1,CE}$: \textcolor{blue}{agent 1 is paid $s(\bar y^{1,CE}-y^1)$}, so \textcolor{blue}{his \emph{effective price of consuming $y^1$ rises} to $p_1+s$}.
$$ \textbf{A1:}\ \max_{y^1,x^1}\ U^1(y^1)+x^1 $$
$$ \text{s.t.}\ \ p_1 y^1+x^1=M_1\textcolor{blue}{+s(\bar y^{1,CE}-y^1)}\quad(\lambda_1), $$
$$ \textbf{A2:}\ \max_{y^2,x^2}\ U^2(y^2)-\varphi(y^1)+x^2 $$
$$ \text{s.t.}\ \ p_2 y^2+x^2=M_2\quad(\lambda_2)\ \text{(unchanged).} $$
\end{keydef} & \begin{keydef} \fcnum{8e}
\textbf{Setting.}
\emph{1)} When agent 1 consumes $y^1$ (gasoline) he creates a negative externality on agent 2.
\emph{2)} Agent 2 has the right to a clean environment and \textcolor{blue}{can sell permits $z$ at price $r$ to use gasoline --- so he \emph{de facto controls} agent 1's consumption. $z^d,z^s$ are permit demand and supply.}
$$ \textbf{A1}\ (y^1,z^d,x^1):\ \max\ U^1(y^1)+x^1 $$
$$ \text{s.t.}\ \ p_1 y^1\textcolor{blue}{+r z^d}+x^1=M_1\quad(\lambda_1),\ \ \textcolor{blue}{y^1\le z^d\quad(\xi_1)}. $$
$$ \textbf{A2}\ (y^1,z^s,x^2):\ \max\ U^2(y^2)-\varphi(y^1)+x^2 $$
$$ \text{s.t.}\ \ p_2 y^2+x^2=M_2\textcolor{blue}{+r z^s}\quad(\lambda_2),\ \ \textcolor{blue}{y^1=z^s\quad(\xi_2)}. $$
\end{keydef} \\
\hline
\textbf{Lagrangian.}
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}={}& U^1(y^1)+x^1+\mu_y(\omega_y-y^1-y^2) \\&+ \mu_x(\omega_x-x^1-x^2)\\ &+\lambda\bigl(U^2(y^2)-\varphi(y^1)+x^2-\bar U\bigr) \end{aligned} $$ & \textbf{Lagrangian} (per agent).
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}^1={}& U^1(y^1)+x^1\\ &-\lambda_1(p_1 y^1+x^1-M_1). \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}^2={}& U^2(y^2)-\varphi(y^1)+x^2\\ &-\lambda_2(p_2 y^2+x^2-M_2). \end{aligned} $$ & \textbf{Lagrangian} (per agent).
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}^1={}& U^1(y^1)+x^1\\ &-\lambda_1\bigl((p_1\textcolor{blue}{+t})y^1+x^1-M_1\textcolor{blue}{-T_1}\bigr). \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}^2={}& U^2(y^2)-\varphi(y^1)+x^2\\ &-\lambda_2(p_2 y^2+x^2-M_2\textcolor{blue}{-T_2}). \end{aligned} $$ & \textbf{Lagrangian.}
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}^1={}& U^1(y^1)+x^1\\ &-\lambda_1\bigl((p_1\textcolor{blue}{+s})y^1+x^1-M_1\textcolor{blue}{-s\,\bar y^{1,CE}}\bigr). \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}^2={}& U^2(y^2)-\varphi(y^1)+x^2\\ &-\lambda_2(p_2 y^2+x^2-M_2). \end{aligned} $$ & \textbf{Lagrangians.}
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}^1={}& U^1(y^1)+x^1\\ &-\lambda_1(p_1 y^1\textcolor{blue}{+r z^d}+x^1-M_1)\\ &\textcolor{blue}{+\xi_1(z^d-y^1)}. \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}^2={}& U^2(y^2)-\varphi(y^1)+x^2\\ &-\lambda_2(p_2 y^2+x^2-M_2\textcolor{blue}{-r z^s})\\ &\textcolor{blue}{+\xi_2(y^1-z^s)}. \end{aligned} $$ \\
\hline
\textbf{FOCs.} $\mu_x=1$ [A], $\lambda=1$ [B]. Then for $y^1$ (symmetric for $y^2$):
$$ \underbrace{\dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1}}_{\text{personal}}+\underbrace{\dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^1}}_{=\,-\varphi'(y^{1*})}=\mu_y $$
Rewritten inline:
$$ \boxed{\;\dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial \textcolor{green}{y^1}}=\textcolor{purple}{\mu_y}+\varphi'(\textcolor{green}{y^{1*}})\;} $$ & \textbf{FOCs.} $\lambda^i=1$, and
$$ \textbf{A1:}\;\dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1}=p_1, \qquad \textbf{A2:}\;\dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^2}=p_2. $$
\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Note: each agent equates own MU to own price. They DO NOT see $\partial U^j/\partial y^i$ --- the spillover on the other agent is ignored.}} & \textbf{FOCs.} $\lambda^i=1$, and
$$ \textbf{A1:}\;\dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1}=\underbrace{p_1}_{=\,\mu_y}+\underbrace{\textcolor{blue}{t}}_{=\,\varphi'(y^{1*})}, \qquad \textbf{A2:}\;\dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^2}=p_2. $$ & \textbf{FOC.} $\lambda_1=1$, and
$$ \dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1}=\underbrace{p_1}_{=\,\mu_y}+\underbrace{\textcolor{blue}{s}}_{=\,\varphi'(y^{1*})}. $$
With $p_1=\mu_y$ and \textcolor{blue}{$s^*=\varphi'(y^{1*})$}: $\dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1}=\mu_y+\varphi'(y^{1*})$ --- the planner condition.
$$ \textbf{A2:}\;\lambda_2=1,\qquad \dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^2}=p_2. $$ & \textbf{Agent 1's FOCs.}
$$ \partial \mathcal{L}^1/\partial x^1:\ 1-\lambda_1=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\textcolor{purple}{\lambda_1}=1}, $$
$$ \textcolor{blue}{\partial \mathcal{L}^1/\partial z^d:\ -\lambda_1 r+\xi_1=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\xi_1=r},} $$
$$ \partial \mathcal{L}^1/\partial y^1:\ \dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1}-\lambda_1 p_1-\xi_1=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1}=p_1\textcolor{blue}{+r}}. $$

\textbf{Agent 2's FOCs.} 
$$ \partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial x^2:\ 1-\lambda_2=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\textcolor{purple}{\lambda_2}=1}, $$
$$ \partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial y^2:\ \dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^2}-\lambda_2 p_2=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial \textcolor{green}{y^2}}=\textcolor{orange}{p_2}}, $$
$$ \textcolor{blue}{\partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial z^s:\ \lambda_2 r-\xi_2=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\xi_2=r},} $$
$$ \textcolor{blue}{\partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial y^1:\ -\varphi'(y^1)+\xi_2=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{r=\varphi'(y^1)}.} $$ \\
\hline
 & \textbf{Result.} No instrument $\Rightarrow$ agent 1 over-consumes $y^1$: private MB $=p_1$ misses the wedge $\varphi'$, so $y^1>y^{1*}$. & \textbf{Discussion.}

\emph{1) Rebate irrelevance (QL).} It is irrelevant to whom you give the revenue. Give the full rebate to agent 1: (i) he does not recognise his $y^1$ funds the rebate (if he did, he'd see there is no net tax and buy the pre-tax quantity); (ii) with QL, a budget expansion does not change interior $y^1$ --- it flows entirely into the numeraire. So the rebate shifts wealth but not post-tax $y^1$; agent 1 still buys less than CE because he pays the extra $t$ at the margin. &  & \textcolor{blue}{1. You need to impose clearing also of the missing market so $z^D = z^S$}
2. \textbf{Why it beats A/B/C.} The market \emph{discovers $r^*$ endogenously} through agent 2's permit supply: the planner need NOT know $\varphi'(y^{1*})$ ex ante --- agent 2 reveals it via his FOC $r=\varphi'(y^1)$. \textcolor{purple}{Caveats: property rights well-defined and enforceable; transaction costs low; breaks with many parties or asymmetric info.} \\
\end{tabular}\emph{1)} If pollution from cars is the negative externality, you tax \emph{pollution}, not cars: a tax on cars alone pushes people to e.g.\ tractors that pollute even more.
\emph{2)} Quotas (Pigou-like). Impose the level of $c$ (consumption / output) directly at the planner's level. \emph{Blunt but works.} Two problems: 1) need to know the exact planner solution and 2) need to monitor (prhibitiionism problem).

nodes.title: Public goods --- taxonomy, distinction from externalities, production model
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Public goods --- taxonomy, distinction from externalities, production model.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Planner vs decentralization (CE with a firm).}}

\begin{tabular}{p{11cm}|p{11cm}}
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{PLANNER}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{CE --- decentralization}} \\
\hline
\begin{keydef} \fcnum{9a}
\textbf{1. Problem.} Choose all quantities to maximize total utility (\emph{same} $y$ enters both):
$$ \max_{x^1,x^2,y,z}\ U^1(x^1,y)+U^2(x^2,y) \text{s.t.}\ \ x^1+x^2+z \;\le\; \omega^1+\omega^2 \quad (\mu), \phantom{\text{s.t.}\ \ } c(y) \;\le\; z \quad (\varphi) $$
\emph{Both constraints bind (idle input wastes utility)} \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} Both bind for sure (monotonicity) --- $\mu,\varphi>0$; nothing to test.
\end{keydef} & \begin{keydef} \fcnum{9b}
\textbf{1. Goal: decentralize the planner allocation via markets.} Now we must also decentralize \emph{production}. The natural modelling choice is to add a \textbf{firm} that produces $y$ (one could instead use voluntary contributions). Prices $p_x,p_y$ (with $p_x$ \emph{not} normalised); firm profit $\pi$ is distributed by ownership shares $\theta^i\ge0$, $\sum_i\theta^i=1$. \emph{Firm} (chooses $y$, sells at $p_y$, input costs $p_x c(y)$):
$$ \max_y\ \pi = p_y\,y - p_x\,c(y). $$
\emph{Consumer $i$} (chooses $x^i$ and contribution $y^i$, with $y=y^1+y^2$):
$$ \max_{x^i,y^i}\ U^i\bigl(x^i,\,y^1+y^2\bigr)  \text{s.t.}\ \ p_x x^i + p_y y^i = p_x\omega^i + \theta^i\pi^* \quad (\lambda^i),  \phantom{\text{s.t.}\ \ } y^i \ge 0 \quad (\xi^i). $$
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} Budget binds for sure (monotonicity, $\lambda^i>0$); $y^i\ge0$ \textcolor{orange}{TO BE TESTED} (no Inada in OWN $y^i$: free-riding can force the corner --- trial in row 3, verification in step (f)).
\end{keydef} \\
\hline
\textbf{2. Lagrangian.}
$$ \mathcal{L} = U^1(x^1,y)+U^2(x^2,y) - \mu\bigl(x^1+x^2+z-\omega^1-\omega^2\bigr) - \varphi\bigl(c(y)-z\bigr). $$ & \textbf{2. Lagrangian.} \emph{Firm: unconstrained (just $\max\pi$), no multiplier.} \emph{Consumer $i$}: budget $\to\lambda^i$, non-negativity $y^i\ge0\to\xi^i$:
$$ \mathcal{L}^i = U^i\bigl(x^i,\,y^1+y^2\bigr)   -\ \lambda^i\bigl(p_x x^i + p_y y^i - p_x\omega^i - \theta^i\pi^*\bigr) + \xi^i\,y^i. $$ \\
\hline
\textbf{3. FOCs.}
$$ \boxed{\tfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial x^1}=\mu},\ \ \boxed{\tfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial x^2}=\mu},\ \ \boxed{\varphi=\mu}, $$
$$ \boxed{\tfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y}+\tfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y}=\mu\,c'(y)}. $$ & \textbf{3. FOCs.} \emph{Firm:}
$$ \boxed{\,p_y = p_x\,c'(y) \iff \tfrac{p_y}{p_x}=c'(y)=MRT\,}. $$
\emph{Consumer $i$} (KKT for the corner $y^i=0$), with $\mathcal{L}^i=U^i-\lambda^i(p_x x^i+p_y y^i-p_x\omega^i-\theta^i\pi^*)+\xi^i y^i$:
$$ \tfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial x^i}=\lambda^i p_x \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\lambda^i=\tfrac{1}{p_x}\tfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial x^i}}, $$
$$ \tfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial y}-\lambda^i p_y+\xi^i=0, $$


\emph{By CS: when the non-negativity constraint is \emph{not} binding there is no marginal value to nudging $y^i>0$ (hence $\xi^i=0$); when it binds, $\xi^i>0$ is the shadow value of the forced $y^i=0$.} (would like to go negative!)

Two cases:
$\bullet$ \emph{Interior} $(\hat y^i>0)$: the $y^i\ge0 \Rightarrow \xi^i=0$ $\rightarrow$ interior FOC at $\hat y$ holds with equality, $\partial U^{-i}/\partial y|_{\hat y} = \lambda^{-i} p_y$. 
$\bullet$ \emph{Boundary} $(\hat y^i=0)$: the constraint binds $\Rightarrow \xi^i>0$ $\rightarrow$ at the SAME $\hat y$, $\dfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial y}\bigg|_{\hat y} \;<\; \lambda^i p_y $

 \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Trial.}} YOU CAN CONJECTURE THE NON INTERIOR REGIME AND VERIFY IT

This means: at consumption 0 the MU of buying one unit is below the price. \textbf{This is not an exception}: whenever the two agents have strictly different MU at $\hat y$, the lower-MU agent free-rides. **Mechanism:** Usually with very low levels of consumption the MU of the first unit is extremely high, in this problem , even if he buys 0 he has high consumption because he is freeriding ont he other agent (it is as if he his starting with higher baseline consumption) \\
\hline
\textbf{4. Samuelson condition (the big FOC).} Divide the last FOC by $\mu=\partial U^i/\partial x^i$:
$$ \boxed{\ \underbrace{\tfrac{\partial U^1/\partial y}{\partial U^1/\partial x^1}}_{MRS^1_{y,x}} + \underbrace{\tfrac{\partial U^2/\partial y}{\partial U^2/\partial x^2}}_{MRS^2_{y,x}} = \underbrace{c'(y)}_{MRT_{y,x}}\ } $$
\emph{Reading:} the planner equates the \textbf{marginal cost of production} $c'(y)$ to the \textbf{social marginal benefit} $=$ the \emph{sum} of agents' MRS. In the quasilinear case ($\mu=1$) the 4th FOC \emph{is} already the Samuelson condition. The 4th FOC also reads as: consuming $y$ costs twice --- the value $\mu$ of each $x$ given up, times $c'(y)$ units of $x$ per unit $y$ (unfavourable technology). & \textbf{5. CE solution path (worked).} General QL: $U^i=x^i+u^i(y)$, cost $c(y)$, agent $1$ the high type ($u_1'>u_2'$ at every $y$), keep $p_x$.
\emph{(a) Merge each agent's two FOCs:} $\partial U^i/\partial x^i=1=\lambda^i p_x\Rightarrow\lambda^i=1/p_x$; then $\partial U^i/\partial y=u_i'(y)=\lambda^i p_y=p_y/p_x \Rightarrow MRS^i=u_i'(y)=p_y/p_x$.
\emph{(b) Firm FOC:} $p_y=p_x c'(y) \Rightarrow p_y/p_x=c'(y)$.
\emph{(c) Combine (a)+(b):} $$ \boxed{\;\; MRS^i_{y,x} \;=\; u_1'(y) \;=\; c'(y) \;=\; MRT \;\; \text{for each contributing agent.}\;\;} $$ So $u_i'(y)=c'(y)$ --- holds for \emph{one} agent only. \textbf{KEEP} the high type's ($i=1$) $y$-FOC; \textbf{DISCARD} the low type's (he corners):
$$ u_1'(y)=c'(y) \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\,y_{CE}\ \text{solves}\ u_1'(y_{CE})=c'(y_{CE})\,},\qquad \dfrac{p_y}{p_x}=c'(y_{CE}). $$
\emph{(e.g. $u^i=a_i\ln y$, $c(y)=\tfrac12 y^2$: $a_1/y=y\Rightarrow y_{CE}=\sqrt{a_1}$, $p_y/p_x=\sqrt{a_1}$.)}
\emph{(d) Contributions:} $y^1=y_{CE}$, $y^2=0$ (agent 1 provides all).
\emph{(e) Profit:} $\pi^*=p_y\,y-p_x c(y)=p_x\bigl(c'(y_{CE})\,y_{CE}-c(y_{CE})\bigr)$; write $\hat\pi\equiv\pi^*/p_x=c'(y_{CE})y_{CE}-c(y_{CE})$.
\emph{(f) Verify the conjectured non-interior regime ($y^2=0$).} Check the discarded FOC: $MRS^2=u_2'(y_{CE})\le p_y/p_x=c'(y_{CE}) \iff u_2'(y_{CE})\le u_1'(y_{CE})$ (true since $1$ is the high type; so $y^2=0$, $\xi^2>0$). Explicitly, from agent 2's $y$-FOC:
$$ \xi^2=\lambda^2 p_y-u_2'(y_{CE})=c'(y_{CE})-u_2'(y_{CE})>0, $$
with $y^2=0$ --- CS consistent ✓. \emph{(e.g. $u^i=a_i\ln y$: $\xi^2=\sqrt{a_1}-\dfrac{a_2}{\sqrt{a_1}}=\dfrac{a_1-a_2}{\sqrt{a_1}}>0$.)}
\emph{(g) Budgets $\Rightarrow$ Marshallian $x^i$} (from $p_x x^i+p_y y^i=p_x\omega^i+\theta^i\pi^*$, divide by $p_x$; use $p_y/p_x=c'(y_{CE})$):
$$ \boxed{\,x^1=\omega^1+\theta^1\hat\pi-c'(y_{CE})\,y_{CE},\qquad x^2=\omega^2+\theta^2\hat\pi.\,} $$
\emph{(h) $x$-market clears} (Walras): $x^1+x^2+c(y)=\omega^1+\omega^2$.
\textcolor{red}{Under-provision: $y_{CE}$ solves $u_1'(y)=c'(y)$ --- only the top type pays; the low type's $u_2'$ never enters $y_{CE}$, whereas the planner's $y^*$ solves $u_1'(y)+u_2'(y)=c'(y)$.} \emph{(Real allocation $x^i,y$ is homogeneous degree $0$ in prices --- independent of the $p_x$ level.)}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The under-provision gap (vs Samuelson).}} Compare with planner:
$$ \text{CE (contributors):}\;\; MRS^i = MRT \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{Planner (Samuelson):}\;\; \sum_i MRS^i = MRT. $$
At CE each agent equates only his OWN MRS to the marginal cost --- he ignores that one more $y$ benefits all agents (non-rivalrous). $\sum_i MRS^i$ exceeds $MRT$ at the CE allocation:
$$ y^{CE} \;<\; y^{*\,\text{Planner}}. $$ \\
\hline
\textbf{5. Planner solution (QL benchmark).} Samuelson $\sum_i MRS^i=MRT$ with $MRS^i=u_i'(y)$, $MRT=c'(y)$: $u_1'(y)+u_2'(y)=c'(y)$ pins $y^*$; the planner \emph{sums} both benefits, so \emph{both} agents enter. \emph{(e.g. $u^i=a_i\ln y$, $c(y)=\tfrac12 y^2$: $\tfrac{a_1+a_2}{y}=y\Rightarrow \boxed{\,y^*=\sqrt{a_1+a_2}\,}$.)} &  \\
\end{tabular}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Public goods --- three classical solutions to under-provision.}}









\emph{From the CE snippet: each contributor sets $MRS^i = p_y/p_x$, but Samuelson requires $\sum_i MRS^i = p_y/p_x = MRT$. Gap: $y^{CE} < y^{*\,Planner}$. Three classical fixes restore Pareto-optimality.}



\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{A. Quota (direct mandate).}} Government mandates each agent's contribution $\bar y^i$ such that $\sum_i \bar y^i = y^*$ (the Samuelson level). Each agent has no choice: $y^i = \bar y^i$, the rest of his income goes to $x^i$.

\emph{Issues:} (1) planner must know $y^*$ and the right distribution of contributions; (2) enforcement / compliance

\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{B. Public provision via lump-sum tax.}} Government directly produces $y^*$ at cost $p_x\, c(y^*)$ and finances it with lump-sum taxes $T^i$ on agents, with $\sum_i T^i = p_x\, c(y^*)$ (balanced budget).

\emph{Each agent's budget:} $p_x x^i = p_x \omega^i + \theta^i \pi^* - T^i$ (no choice on $y$, just on $x^i$).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{C and D --- decentralising the planner: bilateral subsidy vs its tax equivalent.}} \emph{(\textcolor{purple}{purple} $=$ what is new relative to the plain CE.)}. Good because allows **DECENTRALIZATION**

\begin{tabular}{p{11.5cm}|p{11.5cm}}
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{C. Bilateral subsidy}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{D. Tax equivalent}} \\
\hline
\textbf{1. Define the instrument.} When agent $i$ adds a unit of $y^i$, total $\hat y$ rises by $1$, benefiting every OTHER agent --- a positive externality the CE ignores. Subsidise $i$ by the marginal external benefit he creates for the others (per unit of $y^i$):
$$ \textcolor{purple}{s^i} = p_x \sum_{j\ne i} MRS^j\Big|_{\hat y}, $$
where $MRS^j=\dfrac{\partial U^j/\partial y}{\partial U^j/\partial x^j}$ is agent $j$'s dollar value of one unit of $y$ (
Intuitively: the total dollars all OTHER agents together would pay for one more unit of the public good that $i$ provides.

\textcolor{blue}{\emph{Why give the subsidy to everyone.}} A free-rider declines a unit privately because $u_i'(y)<c'(y)$ --- his private bang-for-buck on $y$ is below that of the quasilinear good $x$, so he'd rather buy $x$. But one unit of $y$ benefits \emph{all} agents at once, so its social marginal benefit is $\sum_i u_i'(y)$, which can exceed $c'(y)$ even when \emph{every} agent free-rides individually. \emph{E.g.} $c'(y)=10$, $u_1'=6,\ u_2'=4,\ u_3'=3$: nobody pays alone ($6,4,3<10$), yet socially $6+4+3=13>10$ --- sacrificing $10$ units of $x$ for one more $y$ yields benefits worth $13$. The subsidy $\textcolor{purple}{s^i}=\sum_{j\ne i}u_j'(y)$ hands each agent the others' willingness-to-pay, turning his private margin into the social one. \textcolor{blue}{\emph{How the purchase decision works.}} Agents decide how much $y$ to buy and the firm produces anticipating this. When agent $i$ picks his contribution he weighs the marginal utility of one more unit of $y$ against that of the numeraire $x$ --- \emph{net of the subsidy}. Since the subsidy hands him exactly the external benefit he creates, free-riding buys him nothing: he funds $y$ not out of his own pocket but with a flexible subsidy, so withholding gains him zero. \emph{Who} buys is then indeterminate: with quasilinear utility only the \textbf{total} $\hat y$ is pinned down (Samuelson $\sum_k u_k'(\hat y)=c'(\hat y)$), and any split of contributions summing to $\hat y^*$ is an equilibrium --- if one agent moves first and buys all of $\hat y^*$ that is equally optimal, because at $\hat y^*$ every agent's subsidised FOC holds with equality and the numeraire $x$ absorbs the rest. & \textbf{1. Define the instrument.} Deliver the \emph{same} wedge with a \textbf{tax}. Shortfall tax (D.2): charge $\textcolor{purple}{t^i}(y^*-y^i)$ with $\textcolor{purple}{t^i}=s^i$. \\
\hline
\begin{keydef} \fcnum{9c}
\textbf{2. Problem, utility, budget.} $U^i=a_i\ln \hat y+x^i$ (utility \emph{unchanged}).
$$ \max_{x^i,y^i}\ a_i\ln\hat y+x^i \quad\text{s.t.} $$
$$ p_x x^i + \bigl(p_y-\textcolor{purple}{s^i}\bigr)y^i = p_x\omega^i+\theta^i\pi^*\ (\lambda^i),\quad y^i\ge0\ (\xi^i),\quad i=1,2. $$
\textcolor{purple}{New: the effective price of $y^i$ falls to $p_y-s^i$.}
$$ \boxed{\,\textstyle\sum_i L^i=\sum_i \textcolor{purple}{s^i}y^i\ \text{(GOV BC)}\,} $$
The subsidy outlay must be financed by lump-sum taxes $L^i$ added to the budgets; being lump-sum they are constants $\Rightarrow$ drop from the FOCs, and with QL they hit only $x^i$ --- Samuelson and $\hat y^*$ are untouched, but without them the $x$-market/Walras check fails (the subsidy would inject unbacked wealth $\sum_i s^i y^i$).
\end{keydef} & \textbf{2. Problem, utility, budget.} $U^i=a_i\ln \hat y+x^i$ (unchanged). Shortfall-tax:
$$ \max_{x^i,y^i}\ a_i\ln\hat y+x^i \quad\text{s.t.} $$
$$ p_x x^i + \bigl(p_y-\textcolor{purple}{t^i}\bigr)y^i = p_x\omega^i+\theta^i\pi^*-\textcolor{purple}{t^i y^*}\ (\lambda^i),\quad y^i\ge0\ (\xi^i). $$
\textcolor{purple}{New: same price wedge $-t^i$ on $y^i$, PLUS a lump-sum hit $-t^i y^*$.}
$$ \boxed{\,R=\textstyle\sum_i \textcolor{purple}{t^i}(y^*-y^i)\ \text{rebated lump-sum (GOV BC)}\,} $$
Symmetrically, the collected revenue $R$ must be rebated lump-sum. Once BOTH budgets are closed (tax-finance C, rebate D), C and D with $t^i=s^i$ are equivalent \emph{including} wealth effects --- the "tax makes agents poorer, subsidy richer" contrast below is an artifact of comparing an unfunded subsidy with an unrebated tax. \\
\hline
\textbf{3. Lagrangian.}
$$ \mathcal{L}^i = U^i(x^i,\hat y) - \lambda^i\bigl(p_x x^i + (p_y-\textcolor{purple}{s^i})y^i - p_x\omega^i-\theta^i\pi^*\bigr) + \xi^i y^i. $$
\textcolor{purple}{Only the coefficient on $y^i$ changed} ($p_y\to p_y-s^i$). & \textbf{3. Lagrangian.}
$$ \mathcal{L}^i = U^i(x^i,\hat y) - \lambda^i\bigl(p_x x^i + (p_y-\textcolor{purple}{t^i})y^i - p_x\omega^i-\theta^i\pi^*+\textcolor{purple}{t^i y^*}\bigr) + \xi^i y^i. $$
\textcolor{purple}{$-t^i y^*$ is a constant} $\Rightarrow$ drops from the FOC (pure wealth effect). \\
\hline
\textbf{4. FOCs (where is Samuelson).} For an interior contributor $y^i>0$, the consumer FOCs are:
$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}^i}{\partial x^i}=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{\partial U^i}{\partial x^i}=\lambda^i p_x,
$$
$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}^i}{\partial y^i}=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{\partial U^i}{\partial y}=\lambda^i(p_y-s^i).
$$

Dividing the $y^i$-FOC by the $x^i$-FOC:
$$
\boxed{
MRS^i_{y,x}\Big|_{\hat y}
=
\frac{\partial U^i/\partial y}{\partial U^i/\partial x^i}\Bigg|_{\hat y}
=
\frac{p_y-s^i}{p_x}
=
\frac{p_y}{p_x}
-
\textcolor{purple}{\sum_{j\ne i}MRS^j_{y,x}\Big|_{\hat y}}
}.
$$
\textcolor{purple}{The new term} pulls the free-riders' MRS onto $i$'s margin. Move it over $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{Samuelson}:
$$ \boxed{\;\textcolor{purple}{\sum_k MRS^k\Big|_{\hat y}}=\dfrac{p_y}{p_x}=c'(y)=MRT\;} $$
note: it is not possible to pin down who is gonna buy how much of y (they have the same SMB and consume the same stuff. Rule: is this a sequential game? (...then you know:if you make the game sequential the first guy buys all)) & \textbf{4. FOCs.} $\partial\mathcal{L}^i/\partial x^i:\ \partial U^i/\partial x^i=\lambda^i p_x$; $\partial\mathcal{L}^i/\partial y^i$:
$$ \tfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial y}=\lambda^i\bigl(p_y-\textcolor{purple}{t^i}\bigr)\ \Rightarrow\ MRS^i\Big|_{\hat y}=\dfrac{p_y-t^i}{p_x}. $$
With $\textcolor{purple}{t^i=s^i}$ this is \textbf{identical} to C $\Rightarrow$ same $\sum_k MRS^k=p_y/p_x=MRT$ (Samuelson). The $-t^i y^*$ never entered. \\
\hline
\textbf{5. Solve (QL: $c(y)=\tfrac12 y^2$, $p_x=p_y=1$).} $MRS^i=a_i/\hat y$, $s^i=a_{-i}/\hat y$. Each FOC: $a_i/\hat y=1-s^i=1-a_{-i}/\hat y$. Sum both agents:
$$ \dfrac{a_1+a_2}{\hat y}=2-\dfrac{a_1+a_2}{\hat y}\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\textcolor{purple}{\hat y=\sqrt{a_1+a_2}=y^*}}. $$
\textcolor{purple}{Gap closed:} plain CE gave $y^{CE}=\sqrt{a_1}$ (only the top type provides); the subsidy restores the planner's $\sqrt{a_1+a_2}$. & \textbf{5. Solve.} With $t^i=s^i=a_{-i}/\hat y$ the FOCs are those of C $\Rightarrow$ same
$$ \boxed{\hat y=\sqrt{a_1+a_2}=y^*}. $$
\textcolor{purple}{Identical allocation}; the tax differs only in the wealth effect ($-t^i y^*$ makes agents poorer, the subsidy richer). \\
\end{tabular}
