nodes.title: Martingale property
nodes.content:
gskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Martingale property of Bayesian beliefs.}}












3. The above implies information has to be a priori unpredictable to have value. Indeed, if you know what will happen (probabioty = certianty) this means pg = 1 : $\mathbb{E}[\mu_s] = 1 \mu_g \;=\; \mu_0.\ $  and $\mu_g \;=\; \mu_0$

4. To have martingale holding and information beign valable, you need  $p(g), p(i) \in (0,1)$, this will lead to  $\mu_i < \mu_0 < \mu_g$. Recalling we need $p(i) + p(g) = 1$. As one signal becomes rare ($\Pr(g) \to 0$, say), the corresponding posterior $\mu_g$ jumps far from theprior (huge surprise), while the other ($\mu_i$) barely moves — exactly the $1/\Pr(g)$ surprise factor from earlier.                                                                       
 

Remark: unpredictability is necessary but not sufficient for the spread. If $\alpha = 1/2$, then $\Pr(g), \Pr(i) \in (0,1)$ — the signal is genuinely random — but it's independent of $\omega$, so $\mu_g = \mu_i = \mu_0$. Randomness alone is noise!             


Martignale fixes a rigged experiment: 

Example:

$$
\Pr(g \mid G) = 0.99,
$$

The experiment almost always produces $g$.

$$
\Pr(g \mid I) = 0.90.
$$

Many people would call this ``rigged.''

**But Bayesianly, there is no problem**. If you know these probabilities, then your prior and Bayes' rule already account for them.

The martingale property still holds:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\mu_s] = \mu_0.
$$

Problem is if judge misperceives the probabilities!!!!!!

nodes.title: 3 states 3 signals
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setting.}} Three states $\Omega = \{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}$, three actions $\mathscr{A} = \{a_1, a_2, a_3\}$, three signals $S = \{s_1, s_2, s_3\}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Comparing 2-state and 3-state cases side by side.}}

\begin{tabular}{p{9cm}|p{14cm}|p{14cm}}
\textbf{Quantity --- theory} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{2 states / 2 actions (judge)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{3 states / 3 actions}} \\ \hline

\textbf{Belief} $\mu$ over states.
& $\mu = \Pr(\omega = G) \in [0,1]$ \;(scalar, 1-D)
& $\mu = (\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3)$ on 2-simplex \;($\mu_i \ge 0$, $\sum\mu_i = 1$)
\\ \hline

\textbf{Payoff matrix} $u(a, \omega)$ (diagonal = correct).
& $u(A,I) = u(C,G) = 1$, off-diagonal $= 0$.
& $u(a_i, \omega_j) = \mathbf{1}\{i = j\}$ (diagonal identity).
\\ \hline

\textbf{$U(a, \mu)$ --- expected payoff of action $a$ at belief $\mu$.}
\[
U(a, \mu) = \sum_\omega \mu(\omega)\,u(a, \omega)
\]
\emph{Linear in $\mu$.} One line per action.
&
$U(A, \mu) = (1-\mu)\cdot 1 + \mu \cdot 0 = 1-\mu$ \newline
$U(C, \mu) = (1-\mu)\cdot 0 + \mu \cdot 1 = \mu$ \newline
\emph{2 lines, slopes $\mp 1$, cross at $\mu = 1/2$.}
&
\emph{Show the computation for $a_1$ (others identical):} \newline
$U(a_1, \mu) = \mu_1\,\underbrace{u(a_1,\omega_1)}_{=\,1} + \mu_2\,\underbrace{u(a_1,\omega_2)}_{=\,0} + \mu_3\,\underbrace{u(a_1,\omega_3)}_{=\,0} = \mu_1$. \newline
By symmetry: $U(a_2, \mu) = \mu_2$, $U(a_3, \mu) = \mu_3$. \newline
\emph{Each action action $a_i$ a payoff $\mu_i$}
\\ \hline

\textbf{Value function} $U(\mu) = \max_a U(a, \mu)$. \;Why? Rational DM picks the best action available at belief $\mu$. So i take the best action given my belief :
\[
a^*(\mu) = \arg\max_a U(a, \mu)
\]
$U(\mu)$ = payoff of whichever action is optimal, not of any fixed action.
&
$U(\mu) = \max\{1-\mu,\; \mu\}$ \newline
\emph{V-shape, kink at $\mu = 1/2$.} \newline
$a^*(\mu) = A$ if $\mu < 1/2$, else $C$.
&
$U(\mu) = \max\{\mu_1,\; \mu_2,\; \mu_3\}$ \newline
\emph{Tent with 3 facets on the 2-simplex.} \newline
$a^*(\mu) = a_i$ where $\mu_i$ is the largest coordinate.
\\ \hline

\textbf{Geometric reading.} Plot $U(a, \mu)$ for each action; at each $\mu$ the DM picks the highest line; $U(\mu)$ traces the \textbf{upper envelope}. Below the envelope $=$ sub-optimal. Upper envelope of linear functions $\Rightarrow$ \emph{piecewise linear, convex}, with kinks where the optimal action switches.
&
Two crossing lines $\to$ V-shape upper envelope. 1 kink at $\mu = 1/2$.
&
Three crossing planes on the simplex $\to$ tent upper envelope. 3 indifference lines meeting at the centroid $(1/3, 1/3, 1/3)$ where $U = 1/3$ (most uncertain).
\\ \hline

\textbf{Corner values.}
& $U(\mu = 0) = 1$ (sure innocence, acquit), $U(\mu = 1) = 1$ (sure guilt, convict), $U(\mu = 1/2) = 1/2$ (most uncertain).
& $U(\mu = e_i) = 1$ for each vertex (sure state), $U(\mu = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3)) = 1/3$ (most uncertain).
\\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{purple}{Pattern.}} Same logic in both cases: \emph{each action gives a linear payoff in beliefs; the value function picks the highest one}. Number of states/actions changes the geometry (V-shape $\to$ tent), but the convex piecewise-linear structure is identical. The plot below makes this concrete with 3 lines.

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two extreme information structures $\pi(s\mid\omega)$.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(A) Perfectly informative.}} Identity matrix: each signal reveals the state.

\begin{tabular}{p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}}
$\pi(s\mid\omega)$ & $\omega_1$ & $\omega_2$ & $\omega_3$ \\
\hline
$s_1$ & $1$ & $0$ & $0$ \\
\hline
$s_2$ & $0$ & $1$ & $0$ \\
\hline
$s_3$ & $0$ & $0$ & $1$ \\
\end{tabular}

Posterior = degenerate on the true state. Action always matches. $U_{\text{info}} = 1$.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(B) Perfectly uninformative.}} Columns all equal: signal independent of state.

\begin{tabular}{p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}}
$\pi(s\mid\omega)$ & $\omega_1$ & $\omega_2$ & $\omega_3$ \\
\hline
$s_1$ & $q_1$ & $q_1$ & $q_1$ \\
\hline
$s_2$ & $q_2$ & $q_2$ & $q_2$ \\
\hline
$s_3$ & $q_3$ & $q_3$ & $q_3$ \\
\end{tabular}

with $q_1+q_2+q_3 = 1$. Posterior = prior, regardless of signal. $U_{\text{info}} = U(\mu_0)$ --- no lift.

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Value function as upper envelope of linear utilities.}}

For each action $a$, $U(a, \mu)$ is a \emph{straight line} in $\mu$. The value function $U(\mu) = \max_a U(a, \mu)$ is the \textbf{upper envelope (red)} --- pick whichever line is highest at the current $\mu$.

{{img:0|w=900}}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Reading.}} Three dashed lines = three actions: $U(a_1) = 1-\mu$ (best at low $\mu$), $U(a_2) = 0.6$ (best in the middle), $U(a_3) = \mu$ (best at high $\mu$). The red curve is the upper envelope; the kinks at $\mu = 0.4$ and $\mu = 0.6$ are the \emph{indifference points} where the optimal action switches. \emph{Convex, piecewise linear, three facets} --- same logic as the V-shape for 2 actions, extended to any number of actions.

nodes.title: First Best vs Second Best screening: Mussa--Rosen complete table (book ch.\ 6)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First-best vs second-best screening: complete side-by-side (Mussa--Rosen).}}

\emph{Setting.} Monopolist airline facing two passenger types:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Frugal / leisure type} $\theta_1$ (low marginal value of quality).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Sophisticated / business type} $\theta_2 > \theta_1$ (high marginal value).

Each type's utility from a bundle (quality $q$, fare $t$) is \textbf{quasi-linear}:
$$ U_i(q, t) \;=\; \theta_i\, q \;-\; t. $$
Outside option normalised to $0$. Cost $C(q)$ is convex with $C(0) = C'(0) = 0$ and $\lim_{q\to\infty} C'(q) = \infty$. Probability of frugal is $\pi$.

\emph{Read.} $\theta_i q$ = value of a flight of quality $q$ to type $i$; $t$ = fare paid. Higher $\theta_2$ means \emph{steeper indifference curve} in $(q,t)$-space (sophisticated will pay more for the same quality bump) --- this is the \textbf{Single Crossing Property} / Spence--Mirrlees.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Method note --- how to find which constraints bind.}} Two ways: \textbf{(1) Guess and verify with KKT} (as usual): conjecture a binding pattern, solve, check all multiplier signs and slack constraints ex post. \textbf{(2) PROVE which constraints bind or not} before optimizing (a series of claims), substitute them, and solve a free maximization. \textcolor{red}{In this chapter we ALWAYS go for (2).} The only things (2) leaves to verify ex post are what the proof USED but did not establish: monotonicity $q_2\ge q_1$ and interiority $q_1>0$ (last row).

\begin{tabular}{p{5cm}|p{13cm}|p{13cm}|p{17cm}}
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{First Best (firm OBSERVES type)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{No differentiation (ONE bundle for both)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Second Best (firm CANNOT observe type)}} \\
\hline
\textbf{Problem} & $$ \max_{q_i, t_i}\; t_i - C(q_i) \quad \text{s.t.}\;\; \theta_i q_i - t_i \ge 0\; (\text{IR}_i),\;\; i=1,2. $$
One IR per type; the firm tailors a separate offer to each.
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} IR$_i$ binds \textbf{for sure}: profit is strictly increasing in $t_i$, so the firm raises $t_i$ until IR$_i$ is tight. Nothing to test beyond multiplier signs. & One contract $(q,t)$ for everyone: $\max\ t-C(q)$ s.t. $\theta_1 q-t\ge0$ (IR$_1$, the tighter one --- IR$_2$ is then automatic since $\theta_2>\theta_1$). & $$ \max_{q_1, t_1, q_2, t_2}\; \pi\bigl(t_1 - C(q_1)\bigr) + (1-\pi)\bigl(t_2 - C(q_2)\bigr) $$
s.t.\ $\textbf{IR}_1, \textbf{IR}_2$ AND $\textbf{IC}_1: \theta_1 q_1 - t_1 \ge \theta_1 q_2 - t_2$, $\textbf{IC}_2: \theta_2 q_2 - t_2 \ge \theta_2 q_1 - t_1$.
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Which constraints bind --- PROVED.}} On each type some constraint binds (profit strictly increasing in each $t_i$). Four claims:
(i) \emph{IR$_2$ slack (implied):} $\theta_2 q_2-t_2\ \ge\ \theta_2 q_1-t_1\ \ge\ \theta_1 q_1-t_1\ \ge\ 0$ (IC$_2$, then $\theta_2>\theta_1$, then IR$_1$).
(ii) \emph{IR$_1$ binds:} else raise BOTH $t_1,t_2$ by $\varepsilon$ --- ICs unchanged, IRs still hold, profit strictly up.
(iii) \emph{IC$_2$ binds:} else raise $t_2$ alone by $\varepsilon$ (IR$_2$ slack by (i)) --- profit strictly up.
(iv) \emph{IC$_1$ redundant GIVEN $q_2\ge q_1$:} IC$_2$ binding $\Rightarrow t_2-t_1=\theta_2(q_2-q_1)\ge\theta_1(q_2-q_1)$.
So $\lambda_1,\mu_2>0$, $\lambda_2=\mu_1=0$; drop $q_2\ge q_1$ and \textbf{verify it ex post} (last row). \\
\hline
\textbf{Lagrangian (multipliers).} & Per type $i$, IR$_i$ multiplier $\lambda_i$: $\mathcal{L}_i = t_i - C(q_i) + \lambda_i(\theta_i q_i - t_i)$. & Same one-type Lagrangian as FB, with $\theta_1$: $\mathcal{L}=t-C(q)+\lambda(\theta_1 q-t)$. & Multipliers IR$_1\!\to\!\lambda_1$, IR$_2\!\to\!\lambda_2$, IC$_1\!\to\!\mu_1$, IC$_2\!\to\!\mu_2$:
$$ \mathcal{L} = \pi\bigl(t_1-C(q_1)\bigr)+(1-\pi)\bigl(t_2-C(q_2)\bigr) + \lambda_1(\theta_1 q_1 - t_1) + \lambda_2(\theta_2 q_2 - t_2) + \mu_1\bigl[(\theta_1 q_1 - t_1)-(\theta_1 q_2 - t_2)\bigr] + \mu_2\bigl[(\theta_2 q_2 - t_2)-(\theta_2 q_1 - t_1)\bigr]. $$ \\
\hline
\textbf{FOCs (by type) $\to$ substitute pattern $\to$ quality at the optimum} & FOCs: $\partial_{t_i}\!: 1-\lambda_i=0\Rightarrow\lambda_i=1$; $\partial_{q_i}\!: \lambda_i\theta_i - C'(q_i)=0$; IR$_i$ binds. $\Rightarrow$ $C'(q_i)=\theta_i$. Pattern proved at setup; $\lambda_i=1>0$ consistent with IR$_i$ binding (CS).
\textbf{Both types efficient:} $\boxed{C'(q_i^{FB}) = \theta_i}$ for $i = 1, 2$. \;The marginal cost of quality equals the marginal value to the type buying it. & $\lambda=1$, $C'(q)=\theta_1$ $\Rightarrow$ everyone gets $B$: $\boxed{q=q_1^{FB},\ t=\theta_1 q_1^{FB}}$. & One FOC per choice variable ($t_1,t_2,q_1,q_2$):
$$ \partial_{t_1}:\ \pi-\lambda_1-\mu_1+\mu_2=0, \qquad \partial_{t_2}:\ (1-\pi)-\lambda_2+\mu_1-\mu_2=0, $$
$$ \partial_{q_1}:\ -\pi C'(q_1)+(\lambda_1+\mu_1)\theta_1-\mu_2\theta_2=0, \qquad \partial_{q_2}:\ -(1-\pi)C'(q_2)+(\lambda_2+\mu_2)\theta_2-\mu_1\theta_1=0. $$
Now substitute the proven pattern $\lambda_2=\mu_1=0$ ($\lambda_1,\mu_2>0$, \textbf{proved in row 1}):
$$ \partial_{t_2}\Rightarrow\boxed{\mu_2=1-\pi}, \qquad \partial_{t_1}\Rightarrow\boxed{\lambda_1=\pi+\mu_2=1}; $$
substitute into $\partial_{q_2},\partial_{q_1}$: \textbf{Frugal degraded, soph.\ untouched:}
$$ \boxed{C'(q_2^{SB}) = \theta_2} \;\;\text{(\textbf{no distortion at the top})} $$
$$ \boxed{C'(q_1^{SB}) = \theta_1 - \tfrac{1-\pi}{\pi}(\theta_2 - \theta_1)} \;\;\text{(\textbf{downward distortion at the bottom})} $$
$q_1^{SB} < q_1^{FB}$, $q_2^{SB} = q_2^{FB}$. \\
\hline
\textbf{Fares} & \textbf{Full extraction:} $t_i^{FB} = \theta_i q_i^{FB}$.\;Each type pays their full WTP; both IRs bind. & $t=\theta_1 q$: type 1 fully extracted; type 2 keeps $\textcolor{green}{(\theta_2-\theta_1)q_1^{FB}}$ --- unpriced surplus. & \textbf{Frugal: zero surplus, IR$_1$ binds.} $t_1^{SB} = \theta_1 q_1^{SB}$. \newline
\textbf{Business: rent left on the table, IC$_2$ binds.} $t_2^{SB} = \theta_2 q_2^{SB} - \underbrace{(\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1^{SB}}_{\text{information rent}}$. \newline
The bracket is exactly what business would gain by mimicking leisure --- the firm has to leave it. \\
\hline
\textbf{Buyer surplus} & $0$ for both types. & $U_1=0$, \quad $U_2=(\theta_2-\theta_1)q_1^{FB}>0$. & $U_1^{SB} = 0$ (frugal, IR binds). $U_2^{SB} = (\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1^{SB} > 0$ (business earns the rent). \\
\hline
\textbf{VERIFICATION --- only what the proof did not establish} & Nothing left to verify: pattern proved; $q_i^{FB}$ interior by $C'(0)=0<\theta_i$, $C'\to\infty$ ✓. & --- & \emph{Why this row exists even after the proof: the proof is sufficient for the BINDING PATTERN (multiplier signs and slack constraints need no re-check), but claim (iv) USED $q_2\ge q_1$ without establishing it, and the relaxed problem dropped that constraint --- so it must be checked on the solution.}
\textbf{Monotonicity} (USED in claim (iv), not established): on the solution, $C'(q_2^{SB})=\theta_2>\theta_1-\tfrac{1-\pi}{\pi}(\theta_2-\theta_1)=C'(q_1^{SB})$ and $C'$ increasing $\Rightarrow q_2^{SB}>q_1^{SB}$ ✓ --- so IC$_1$ holds and the proof closes. \textbf{Interiority} of $q_1^{SB}$: needs $\theta_1-\tfrac{1-\pi}{\pi}(\theta_2-\theta_1)>0$. \textcolor{red}{If it FAILS (gap $\theta_2-\theta_1$ too big or $\pi$ too small), the interior solution breaks at the FOC level: $C'(q_1)\le0$ impossible. Fix: corner $q_1^{SB}=0$ --- EXCLUDE the frugal type --- and re-solve: serve business only, $q_2=q_2^{FB}$, $t_2=\theta_2 q_2^{FB}$; verify the new regime: $\mu_2\ge0$ ✓, exclusion IC trivially ✓.} \\
\hline
\textbf{Why this allocation?} & Types observable $\Rightarrow$ no defection possible. Set $q$ at the tangency $C'(q) = \theta_i$ and charge full WTP. The point in $(q,t)$-space is the tangency between the firm's iso-profit curve and the type's indifference curve through the origin. & No screening instruments used at all: the firm gives up on separating the types. & The first-best is \emph{not} IC: at $B$ (frugal's FB bundle), business gets utility $\theta_2 q_1 - t_1 = (\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1 > 0$ --- they would lie and grab B. \newline
Two options to restore IC:
$\bullet$ Cut $t_2$ to give business the same surplus they'd get at B (still $q_2 = q_2^{FB}$). \emph{Costs rent, no efficiency loss.}
$\bullet$ Reduce $q_1$ (degrade economy) so that B is less attractive for business. \emph{Saves rent, but distorts leisure away from efficiency.}
Optimum: \textbf{both at once} until $\pi(\theta_1 - C'(q_1)) = (1-\pi)(\theta_2 - \theta_1)$. \\
\hline
\textbf{Plot} & {{img:3|w=620}} & {{img:4|w=620}} & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(1) ICs ignored (FB menu offered) $\to$ type 2 defects:}}
{{img:5|w=620}}
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(2) ICs bind (true second best):}}
{{img:6|w=620}} \\
\hline
\textbf{Reading the plot} & $A = $ sophisticated bundle, $B = $ frugal bundle. Indifference curves pass through origin (IR binds = zero buyer surplus). Iso-profit curves $t = \bar\Pi + C(q)$ are convex. \textbf{Tangency} between IC and iso-profit $\Rightarrow$ $C'(q_i^*) = \theta_i$ (slope of IC equals slope of iso-profit). \textbf{Production efficiency, full extraction.} & Both types sit at $B$. \textcolor{green}{Green segment above $B$ up to the $\theta_2$ line $=$ CS$_2$}; \textcolor{red}{red $=$ PS}; \textbf{black triangle $=$ DWL}: type 2 stuck at $q_1^{FB}<q_2^{FB}$. & $A \to A'$: same quality $q_2$, but the fare drops by the rent $(\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1^{SB}$ so business is willing to stay. \newline
$B \to B'$: reduce $q_1$ and $t_1$ along the frugal's indifference curve (IR$_1$ stays binding, $U_1 = 0$). Lower $q_1$ shrinks the rent $(\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1$ that business would steal at B --- saving on $A'$. The optimal trade-off equates the marginal saved-rent on business to the marginal lost-profit on frugal. \\
\hline
\textbf{DWL} & $0$. Both types served efficiently, surplus fully transferred (not destroyed). & $>0$: type 2 consumes $q_1^{FB}$ instead of $q_2^{FB}$. & $> 0$. Frugal's missing quality $q_1^{FB} - q_1^{SB}$ destroys real surplus. \textbf{The DWL is the price of asymmetric information.} \\
\hline
\textbf{Comparative statics} & $q_i^{FB}$ depends only on $(\theta_i, C(\cdot))$ --- not on type distribution. & --- & $q_1^{SB}$ decreases in $(\theta_2 - \theta_1)$ (bigger type gap $\Rightarrow$ stronger temptation $\Rightarrow$ more degradation needed). \newline
$q_1^{SB}$ decreases in $\frac{1-\pi}{\pi}$ (more sophisticated relative to frugal $\Rightarrow$ rents matter more $\Rightarrow$ more aggressive degradation). \newline
\emph{Reading: the firm is willing to sacrifice profits on each frugal customer in proportion to how many sophisticated customers it can extract more from.} \\
\hline
\textbf{Mussa--Rosen logic in one line} & First best $=$ perfect PD: $C'(q_i) = \theta_i, t_i = \theta_i q_i$, $U_i = 0$. & Pooling $=$ the low type's FB applied to everyone: cheap to run, wastes the top's WTP. & Second best $=$ \textbf{degrade the bottom + leave rent at the top}: $\boxed{C'(q_1^{SB}) = \theta_1 - \tfrac{1-\pi}{\pi}(\theta_2 - \theta_1),\;\; t_2^{SB} = \theta_2 q_2^{FB} - (\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1^{SB}}.$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Connection to airline cabins} & If airline could check expense reports: business class at \$2{,}000 (full WTP), economy at \$300 (full WTP). Both fly, no rents leak. & One cabin class for everybody. & Real world: business class \$1{,}700 (after the \$300 rent left to deter defection); economy is \textbf{intentionally degraded} (cramped seat, no upgrades, no lounge access) so business flyers don't even consider it. Leisure gets a strictly worse trip than they would in first best --- that's the DWL. \\
\end{tabular}



\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Step 4 --- it doesn't work naively: business flyers defect.}} A business flyer can fly economy just fine. If economy is cheap and not too bad, they \textbf{buy down}: take the economy ticket, pocket the big surplus instead of paying the high business fare. The menu falls apart.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The key idea behind every screening problem:}} the business flyer's WTP is \emph{higher than the leisure flyer's at every quality level}. Whatever bundle the firm designs for leisure, the business flyer wants it too --- unless something stops them. (Single-crossing / Spence--Mirrlees.)

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Step 5 --- restore incentive compatibility (IC).}} Two instruments to prevent defection:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Cut the business fare} just enough to leave business better off than mimicking economy. The amount by which the fare is cut below full WTP is the \emph{\textbf{information rent}}.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Degrade the economy product} (narrow seat, no flexibility, no lounge) until business flyers don't want it. Cheaper than paying rent, but socially \emph{inefficient} --- leisure flyers get a worse trip than they would in first best.


\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Take-aways.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{No distortion at the top, downward distortion at the bottom.} The high type always gets the efficient quality; only the low type's bundle is shrunk.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Two costs of asymmetric information}: (i) the rent left to the high type, (ii) the DWL from shrinking the low type's quality. The firm chooses the mix that minimises their sum.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Mussa--Rosen trade-off:} $\frac{\partial(\text{rent on } H)}{\partial q_L} \;=\; \frac{\partial(\text{lost profit on } L)}{\partial q_L}$. Lower $q_L$ saves rent but kills surplus on leisure.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Single Crossing is the binding case:} this analysis assumes $H$'s WTP exceeds $L$'s at every $q$ (linear). With sigmoidal / saturating preferences (real life), the IC is naturally slacker and screening gets \textbf{strictly easier}. The linear case is the firm's worst-case scenario.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{OLD PLOTS (for comparison with the new CS/PS/DWL versions above).}}

nodes.title: Asymmetric Information --- intro (adverse selection vs moral hazard)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setting --- asymmetric information.}}

A market or contracting situation involves \textbf{asymmetric information} when one party knows something relevant to the trade that the other does not. The informed side has private knowledge about a \emph{type} (who they are) or an \emph{action} (what they do); the uninformed side can only condition on what is observable.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two canonical forms.}}

The asymmetry shows up in two structurally different ways. The distinction is \emph{when} the private information arises relative to the contract:

\begin{tabular}{p{8cm}|p{15cm}|p{15cm}}
 & \textbf{Adverse Selection (AS)} & \textbf{Moral Hazard (MH)} \\
\hline
\textbf{a) what's hidden} & \emph{Hidden type / hidden characteristic.} The informed party knows who they are (risk class, productivity, quality). & \emph{Hidden action / hidden effort.} The informed party chooses an action the principal cannot observe (or verify in court). \\
\hline
\textbf{b) timing} & \textbf{Pre-contract.} Private info exists \emph{before} the contract is signed. & \textbf{Post-contract.} Action is chosen \emph{after} the contract is signed. \\
\hline
\textbf{c) keyword} & Who am I dealing with? & What will they do? \\
\end{tabular}

\bigskip


\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Reading: why this taxonomy matters.}}

The two problems require different instruments:

$\bullet$ \textbf{AS} is about \emph{sorting} types --- the contract must reveal who the agent is. The principal designs a menu and lets the agent's choice signal type (incentive-compatibility on \emph{types}).

$\bullet$ \textbf{MH} is about \emph{motivating} an action --- the agent's identity is fixed, but his effort must be elicited. The contract ties payment to a noisy signal of effort (incentive-compatibility on \emph{actions}).

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Same mathematical tool, different binding constraint:}} in both cases we solve a constrained optimisation where the IC constraint is what asymmetric information adds on top of the standard participation (IR) constraint. In AS the IC is \emph{across types}; in MH it is \emph{across actions of one agent}.



\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The cost of inducing revelation.}}

Getting types to reveal themselves is not free. The IC constraint forces the principal to leave \emph{information rents} to good types and to \emph{distort the contract of bad types away from first best} so that good types do not want to mimic them.

Resulting inefficiencies:

$\bullet$ \emph{Information rents:} good types are paid more than their reservation utility just to keep them from pooling.

$\bullet$ \emph{Downward distortion at the bottom:} the bad type's allocation (quantity, coverage, quality) is reduced below the efficient level --- this hurts the bad type but slackens the good type's IC, lowering the rent the principal must pay.

$\bullet$ \emph{Exclusion / partial unravelling:} if rents are too costly, the principal drops the worst types from the menu altogether and gains from trade with them vanish.

So the screening menu is \emph{2nd-best}: it is the best one can do given that types are private, but strictly below the symmetric-information first best.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three markets with adverse selection.}}

\begin{tabular}{p{10cm}|p{14cm}|p{14cm}}
\textbf{market} & \textbf{the AS problem} & \textbf{market solution} \\
\hline
\textbf{1) Health insurance} & High-risk individuals know their own risk; insurer doesn't. A single pooled premium attracts the sick and repels the healthy $\Rightarrow$ premium rises $\Rightarrow$ healthy drop out (death spiral). & \emph{Differentiated plans} (menu of deductible/coverage pairs): low deductible at high premium for high-risk, high deductible at low premium for low-risk. Types self-select. \\
\hline
\textbf{2) Used cars (Akerlof)} & Seller knows if the car is a peach or a lemon; buyer doesn't. At the average price peaches won't sell $\Rightarrow$ only lemons trade. & \emph{Third-party screening:} certified inspections (CarFax, mechanic reports), dealer warranties, return policies --- the uninformed side buys a verification technology that converts hidden info into hard info. \\
\hline
\textbf{3) Labour market (Spence)} & Worker knows his productivity; employer doesn't. Pooled wage = average productivity drives high types out. & \emph{Signaling through education/tests:} costly signal (degree, certification, exam) acquired by high types because their cost-per-signal is lower. Wage conditions on the signal and separates types. \\
\end{tabular}

nodes.title: How to perform  PO optimization
nodes.content:
\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{Two characterizations of Pareto Set }}

\begin{keydef} \fcnum{3b}
\emph{Why a planner?} Both characterizations are written from the viewpoint of a benevolent social planner who chooses an allocation $(x_h^1,x_l^1,x_h^2,x_l^2)\in\mathcal F$ to maximize a welfare objective. Two possible characterizations:
$$\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
[\mathrm A]:\qquad
x^*(\lambda)\in
\arg\max_{\substack{x_h^1,x_l^1\geq0 \\ x_h^2,x_l^2\geq0}}
&\ \lambda U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)
+(1-\lambda)U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2) \\
\text{s.t.}\qquad
&x_h^1+x_h^2=\omega_h \quad(\mu_h), \\
&x_l^1+x_l^2=\omega_l \quad(\mu_l), \\
&\lambda\in(0,1).
\end{aligned}}
$$
$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
[\mathrm B]:\qquad
P(\bar u^1)=
\max_{\substack{x_h^1,x_l^1\geq0 \\ x_h^2,x_l^2\geq0}}
&\ U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2) \\
\text{s.t.}\qquad
&U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)\geq\bar u^1 \quad(\gamma), \\
&x_h^1+x_h^2=\omega_h \quad(\mu_h), \\
&x_l^1+x_l^2=\omega_l \quad(\mu_l).
\end{aligned}}
$$
\end{keydef}

\begin{tabular}{p{2.8cm}|p{10.5cm}|p{10.5cm}}
& \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{[A] Linear scalarization --- weighted SWF}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{[B] Constrained maximization --- UPF as an explicit function}} \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{1. Set-up.}} \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} Resource constraints bind for sure (monotonicity, $\mu_h,\mu_l>0$); $x\ge0$ slack for sure (Inada); in [B] the floor $U^1\ge\bar u^1$ binds for sure ($\gamma>0$: $U^2$ strictly increasing $\Rightarrow$ the planner pushes agent 1 to the floor). Nothing to test. &
$$\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
[\mathrm A]:\qquad
x^*(\lambda)\in
\arg\max_{\substack{x_h^1,x_l^1\geq0 \\ x_h^2,x_l^2\geq0}}
&\ \lambda U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)
+(1-\lambda)U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2) \\
\text{s.t.}\qquad
&x_h^1+x_h^2=\omega_h \quad(\mu_h), \\
&x_l^1+x_l^2=\omega_l \quad(\mu_l), \\
&\lambda\in(0,1).
\end{aligned}}
$$ &
$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
[\mathrm B]:\qquad
P(\bar u^1)=
\max_{\substack{x_h^1,x_l^1\geq0 \\ x_h^2,x_l^2\geq0}}
&\ U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2) \\
\text{s.t.}\qquad
&U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)\geq\bar u^1 \quad(\gamma), \\
&x_h^1+x_h^2=\omega_h \quad(\mu_h), \\
&x_l^1+x_l^2=\omega_l \quad(\mu_l).
\end{aligned}}
$$ \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{2. Lagrangian.}} &
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L
=\;&
\lambda U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)
+
(1-\lambda)U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2) \\
&+
\mu_h\bigl(\omega_h-x_h^1-x_h^2\bigr)
+
\mu_l\bigl(\omega_l-x_l^1-x_l^2\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$ &
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L
=\;&
U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2) + \gamma\bigl(U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)-\bar u^1\bigr) \\
&+ \mu_h\bigl(\omega_h-x_h^1-x_h^2\bigr) + \mu_l\bigl(\omega_l-x_l^1-x_l^2\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$ \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{3. FOCs}} &
From the Lagrangian, optimized for the 4 consumption variables $x_h^1,x_l^1,x_h^2, x_l^2$, and the focs are:
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Good $h$ (one FOC per agent, common rhs $\mu_h$):}}
$$\lambda
\underbrace{\frac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_h^1}}_{\text{Agent 1's MU from +1u of consumption}}
=
\underbrace{\mu_h}_{\text{social marginal value of +1u of good }h},
\qquad
(1-\lambda)\frac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_h^2}=\mu_h.
$$
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Good $l$ (common rhs $\mu_l$):}}
$$
\lambda\frac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_l^1}=\mu_l,
\qquad
(1-\lambda)\frac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_l^2}=\mu_l.
$$

\textbf{How you have to frame it:} the planner has his units of h (say he has 30 units):
1) he takes the first unit, and seee the Mu of agent 1 is 50, og agent 2 40, he gives this unit to agent 1
2) then he takes the scond unit, now the mu of agent 1 is 30, of agent 2 40, he gives this unit to agent 1
...
3) now he has his last unit, the marginal utility of agent 1 is muh, the marginal utility of agent 2 is muh + epsilon, he gives this unit to agent 2.
NOTE THAT WHAT YOU HAVE ABOVE IS AN OPTIMALITY CONDITION SAYING: you have to distribute utilities (or for CE: agents will consume up until) until the marginal utility is equal to the shadow value of the cosntraint  (endogenous from the problem!)
\textcolor{purple}{Note how beautiful the math is: the common rhs (across agents) allows you to unify the utility you give to agent 1 to the utility you give to agent 2. This means that $\mu_h$ is gonna be the unified value of consuming good h and $\mu_l$ the unified value of consuming good l. Obviously dependign on the weights and the utility functions the level of these thresholds will change! }

\textcolor{darkgreen}{**MRS**}
Dividing the focs: 
$$\underbrace{\frac{\partial U^1/\partial x_h^1}
{\partial U^1/\partial x_l^1}}_{\mathrm{MRS}_{h,l}^1}
=
\frac{\mu_h}{\mu_l}
=
\underbrace{\frac{\partial U^2/\partial x_h^2}
{\partial U^2/\partial x_l^2}}_{\mathrm{MRS}_{h,l}^1},
$$
This conditions tells you what is the optimal rate of change of good h for good l &
FOCs (4 consumption variables):
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Good $h$:}}
$$ \gamma\frac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_h^1}=\mu_h,\quad \frac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_h^2}=\mu_h. $$
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Good $l$:}}
$$ \gamma\frac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_l^1}=\mu_l,\quad \frac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_l^2}=\mu_l. $$

\textcolor{darkgreen}{**MRS**}

Dividing $\Rightarrow \mathrm{MRS}^1_{h,l}=\dfrac{\mu_h}{\mu_l}=\mathrm{MRS}^2_{h,l}$ --- the \emph{same} Pareto condition as $[\mathrm A]$, with $\gamma$ playing the role of the weight ratio $\lambda/(1-\lambda)$.
Different approach, same result! \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{4. How to read the FOCs.}} &
 &
 \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{5. Result --- MRS condition.}} &
 &
 \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{6. Geometry --- tracing the UPF.}} &
$\bullet$ Note how in the isowelfare space the welfare line $ W = \lambda U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1) +(1-\lambda)U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2)$, solving for $U^2$, has slope $-\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda},$ and its vertical intercept is $ K=\frac{W}{1-\lambda}.$ For a fixed value of $\lambda$, maximizing welfare means moving the isowelfare line outward, parallel to itself, until it reaches the utility-possibility set. If the utility-possibility set is compact and the weighted welfare function is continuous, the Weierstrass theorem guarantees that a max $\exists$. This means that, for every fixed $\lambda$, the weighted social-welfare problem has at least one solution (a PO point, again, existence of a PO point is easy).
$\bullet$ Remark: you need $\lambda \in (0,1)$ since we could have agent i satiation. In case of strict monotonicity this would not be needed
$\bullet$ Varying $\lambda$ traces the supported points of the utility-possibility frontier. {{img:0|w=580}} &
The planner fixes Agent 1 at a utility floor $\bar u^1$ and maximizes Agent 2's utility. By varying $\bar u^1$ over its feasible range,
$$
\bar u^1\in[u_{\min}^1,u_{\max}^1],
$$
the planner traces the utility-possibility frontier as an explicit decreasing function $U^2=P(U^1).$ \\
\end{tabular} 

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Example --- one-good economy.}}

Suppose there is only one good, with total endowment $\omega$, and that $U^i$ is strictly increasing for each agent. Since there is only one good, denote the amount consumed by Agent $i$ simply by $x^i$. The constrained-maximization problem becomes
$$
P(\bar u^1)
=
\max_{x^1,x^2\geq0}
U^2(x^2)
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
U^1(x^1)\geq\bar u^1,
\qquad
x^1+x^2=\omega.
$$

- Strict monotonicity implies that Agent 1's utility constraint binds: $ U^1(x^1)=\bar u^1.$ Therefore $x^1=(U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1).$

- Resource feasibility implies $ x^2 = \omega-x^1 = \omega-(U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1). $

Hence, $\boxed{ P(\bar u^1) = U^2\left( \omega-(U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1) \right)}$

\textbf{Prices and trade in a one-good exchange economy.}

In the two-good economy, the general budget constraint of Agent $i$ is $p_hx_h^i+p_lx_l^i = p_h\omega_h^i+p_l\omega_l^i.$ In a one-good economy, the budget constraint becomes $px^i=p\omega^i $

For any strictly positive price $p>0$, $ x^i=\omega^i $

Thus, each agent can afford only their initial endowment. There is no relative price because there is only one good, and setting $p=1$ is merely a numéraire normalization.

The relevant statement is not that the budget line has slope one: with only one good, the budget set is a point on a one-dimensional consumption space rather than a line in a two-dimensional diagram.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Verification.}} Interior regime: all four FOCs hold with $\mu_h,\mu_l>0$ (and $\gamma>0$ in [B]); demands interior by Inada --- no regime switch needed.

nodes.title: Bayesian Updating
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FINAL COMPARISON --- no information vs information; general formulas vs the two scenarios ($\alpha=0.7$).}}

\begin{tabular}{p{2.2cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}}
 &
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{GENERAL (any $\mu_0$, any $\alpha$)}} &
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{SWITCH scenario: $\mu_0=0.5\in[1-\alpha,\alpha]$, $\alpha=0.7$}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{NO-SWITCH scenario: $\mu_0=0.3=1-\alpha$ (boundary knife edge)}} \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{1. Belief (prior).}} &
A decision maker (DM) --- think of a \emph{judge} --- faces uncertainty over a binary state $\omega \in \Omega = \{I, G\}$ ($I$ = innocent, $G$ = guilty). His belief is summarized by the scalar $\mu_0=\Pr(\omega=G)\in[0,1]$: the judge's prior belief that the suspect is guilty. &
$\mu_0=0.5$: maximal uncertainty --- the belief sits exactly at the cutoff $\hat\mu=1/2$. & $\mu_0=0.3$: lean toward \emph{innocence} --- sitting \emph{exactly at} the lower switch threshold $1-\alpha=0.3$. \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{2. Utilities of the actions (no information).}} &
The judge picks an action $a \in \mathscr{A} = \{A, C\}$ (acquit or convict). Payoffs match action to state: $u = 1$ if he ``gets it right'' and $0$ otherwise.

\emph{Convict:} \;$U(C,\mu) \;=\; (1-\mu)\,\underbrace{u(C,I)}_{=\,0} \;+\; \mu\,\underbrace{u(C,G)}_{=\,1} \;=\; \mu.$

\emph{Acquit:} \;$U(A,\mu) \;=\; (1-\mu)\,\underbrace{u(A,I)}_{=\,1} \;+\; \mu\,\underbrace{u(A,G)}_{=\,0} \;=\; 1-\mu.$

So $U(C,\cdot)$ is linear with slope $+1$ (rewards belief in guilt), and $U(A,\cdot)$ is linear with slope $-1$ (rewards belief in innocence). Plotted together, they form an \textbf{X-shape} crossing at $\mu = 1/2$.


{{img:4|w=520}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4. Information arrives: posteriors and signal probabilities.}} &
\emph{Idea.}  New evidence arrives (an \emph{experiment}: a forensic test, a witness, a database query) producing for each suspect a \textbf{signal} $s \in \{i, g\}$. The experiment is parameterised by a single number $\alpha \in [1/2,\,1]$ (the \emph{informativeness}):
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \Pr(s\mid\omega) & \omega = I & \omega = G \\ \hline s = i & \alpha & 1-\alpha \\ \hline s = g & 1-\alpha & \alpha \end{array}$$
\emph{Each column sums to $1$; the diagonal entries are the correct calls.} $\alpha=1/2$: signal independent of the state $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{no information}. $\alpha=1$: signal reveals the state $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{perfect information}. $\alpha<1/2$: labels flipped; WLOG $\alpha\ge1/2$.
After observing $s = g$, the judge's posterior is by Bayes (joint $=$ conditional $\times$ prior, divided by the marginal):
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_g \;&:=\; \Pr(G \mid g) \;=\; \frac{\Pr(g \mid G)\,\Pr(G)}{\Pr(g \mid G)\,\Pr(G) \;+\; \Pr(g \mid I)\,\Pr(I)} \\
&=\; \frac{\alpha\,\mu_0}{\alpha\,\mu_0 \;+\; (1-\alpha)(1-\mu_0)}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Symmetrically, after observing $s = i$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_i \;&:=\; \Pr(G \mid i) \;=\; \frac{\Pr(i \mid G)\,\Pr(G)}{\Pr(i \mid G)\,\Pr(G) \;+\; \Pr(i \mid I)\,\Pr(I)} \\
&=\; \frac{(1-\alpha)\,\mu_0}{(1-\alpha)\,\mu_0 \;+\; \alpha\,(1-\mu_0)}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $\alpha \ge 1/2$ we always have $\mu_g \ge \mu_0 \ge \mu_i$.
\emph{Signal probabilities (law of total probability --- the two disjoint routes by which each signal can arrive):}
$$ \Pr(g)=\underbrace{\Pr(g\mid G)\,\Pr(G)}_{\substack{\text{from the guilty} \\ \Pr(G)=\mu_0}}+\underbrace{\Pr(g\mid I)\,\Pr(I)}_{\substack{\text{from the innocent} \\ \Pr(I)=1-\mu_0}}=\alpha\mu_0+(1-\alpha)(1-\mu_0),\qquad \Pr(i)=1-\Pr(g). $$::

\emph{At $\mu_0=0.33+0.001$:} \textcolor{blue}{before $U(0.331)=0.669$}; \textcolor{darkgreen}{after unbiased $\alpha=0.7$} (inside the unbiased switch regime); \textcolor{red}{after biased at the prosecutor's optimum $\varepsilon^*\approx0.092$: $\alpha+\varepsilon^*(2\mu_0-1)=0.7-0.092\cdot0.338\approx0.669$} --- \textbf{exactly the no-information baseline: the prosecutor's optimal bias extracts the judge's ENTIRE informational surplus}, pushing him back to indifference (VOI $=0$) while maximising convictions --- precisely the persuasion logic. \\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setting --- the biased information structure.}}



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Comparison table --- unbiased vs biased (at $\mu_0 = 1/2,\;\alpha = 0.7$; biased uses $\varepsilon = 0.1$).}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{THE DARK EDGE CASE at $\mu_0 = 1/2$.}} The Bayesian adjustment in $\mu_g$ corrects per-case logic but \emph{never} prevents conviction as long as $\mu_g \ge 1/2$. So the sender's only constraint is to keep $\mu_g \ge 1/2$. \newline \textbf{Mild bias} ($\varepsilon = 0.1$, this column): conviction rate $50\% \to 60\%$. Innocent-share among convicted $= 1-\mu_g = 33\%$ (up from $30\%$). Already a step toward the dark limit. \newline \textbf{Pushed to the limit:} as the experiment becomes nearly uninformative ($\alpha \to 1/2$) biased toward $g$, we can have $\Pr(g\mid I) \approx \Pr(g\mid G) \approx 0.99$. Then: \newline $\bullet$ $\Pr(g) \approx 0.99 \Rightarrow$ \textbf{99\% of cases get signal $g$}. \newline $\bullet$ $\mu_g \approx \mu_0 = 1/2$ (judge learned nothing; indifferent; tie-breaks to $C$). \newline $\bullet$ \textbf{99\% of the population goes to jail}; half of the convicted are innocent ($1-\mu_g = 1/2$). \newline \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Judge rationality is NOT a defense.}} On every individual case the judge is solving his decision problem optimally --- his per-case expected payoff $U_{\text{info}}^{\text{biased}}(1/2) = \alpha$ is unchanged (see VOI section below). He cannot ``acquit more'' without violating his own utility. The collapse happens at the \emph{population} level, invisible inside any single case. \newline \emph{Fix lives outside the judge:} regulate $\alpha$ (force diagnostic content), or change the tie-break rule (acquit on indifference).










\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Final plot --- conviction probability $P_C(\mu_0)$.}}

Two panels: no bias on the left, bias ($\varepsilon = 0.1$) on the right. Black dashed: no-info baseline. Red: with-info.



\textbf{System for $P_C(\mu_0)$.}
$$
P_C^{\text{unb}}(\mu_0) = \begin{cases} 0 & \mu_0 < 1-\alpha \\ \Pr(g) \;=\; \Pr(g\mid G)\mu_0 + \Pr(g\mid I)(1-\mu_0) \;=\; \underbrace{\Pr(g\mid I)}_{\text{intercept}} + \underbrace{[\Pr(g\mid G) - \Pr(g\mid I)]}_{\text{slope}}\mu_0 \;=\; (1-\alpha) + (2\alpha-1)\mu_0 & 1-\alpha \le \mu_0 < \alpha \\ 1 & \mu_0 \ge \alpha \end{cases}
$$
$$
P_C^{\text{biased}}(\mu_0) = \begin{cases} 0 & \mu_0 < \mu_0^{*L,b} \\ \Pr(g) \;=\; \Pr(g\mid G)\mu_0 + \Pr(g\mid I)(1-\mu_0) \;=\; \underbrace{\Pr(g\mid I)}_{\text{intercept}} + \underbrace{[\Pr(g\mid G) - \Pr(g\mid I)]}_{\text{slope}}\mu_0 \;=\; (1-\alpha+\varepsilon) + (2\alpha-1)\mu_0 & \mu_0^{*L,b} \le \mu_0 < \mu_0^{*U,b} \\ 1 & \mu_0 \ge \mu_0^{*U,b} \end{cases}
$$

nodes.title: Cobb douglas preferences
nodes.content:
**Cobb douglas preferences**
$$
U(x_a,x_b)=\alpha\ln x_a+(1-\alpha)\ln x_b.
$$

**Its Marshallian demands are**
$$
\boxed{
x_a^*=\frac{\alpha w}{p_a},
\qquad
x_b^*=\frac{(1-\alpha)w}{p_b}.
}
$$

Notic ethat
$$
x_a^* \text{ does not depend on } p_b,
\qquad
x_b^* \text{ does not depend on } p_a.
$$

This is \textbf{not a consequence of homotheticity alone}. It is a special property of Cobb--Douglas demand, that is called the \textbf{constant expenditure shares property}:
$$
\boxed{
p_a x_a^*=\alpha w,
\qquad
p_b x_b^*=(1-\alpha)w.
}
$$

::When $p_a$ rises (holding $w$ fixed), the share spent on good $B$ remains exactly fixes: indeed CD is special as well because sub and income effect balance exactly. Therefore, expenditure on $B$ does not change, and since $p_b$ also remains unchanged, the quantity $x_b^*$ does not change either.::

nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{REMARKS.}}
For planner:
6.a) Two cases: 
- $\lambda = 1/2$ and one good is linear. E.g.\ $x$. System will not determine any allocation for $x^i$. The reason: you are indifferent to the agents, of whomever you give the good to, the effect will be the same as the MU is affected in the same way. This does not hold for homothetic goods: even with $\lambda > 1/2$, the concavity of $\ln y$ kicks in: comparing marginal utility at $y = 0.5$ vs.\ $y = 9$, the planner wants to give \emph{more} $y$ to the favored agent --- but at some point diminishing returns make them stop. So the system DOES pin down a unique interior allocation for $y$.

- $\lambda > 1/2$ or $\lambda < 1/2$ $\to$ you care more of one agent you give **ALL** the quasiliniear good to him (the MU is the same).
 

6.b) Whenever you solve $P(u_1) = \max\ldots$ sub $\ldots u_2 \ge \bar u$ you are not agnostic on $y_1^*, y_2^*, x_1^*, x_2^*$ $\to$ system will pin down these quantities both in homothetic cases and in cases with quasi-linear  goods.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{QUASILINEAR PREFERENCES --- CE vs PLANNER (one table, four parallel tracks).}}

\begin{tabular}{p{8.5cm}|p{8.5cm}|p{8.5cm}|p{8.5cm}}
\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{\textcolor{red}{QUASILINEAR PREFERENCES --- CE solution (worked, two endowment configurations).}}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{PLANNER --- weighted SWF (aggregate resources)}}} \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CE --- no slack}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{CE --- slack (agent endowments)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{PO --- no slack}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{PO --- slack (Planner choice)}} \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Case 1: $\omega^1=(9,9)$, $\omega^2=(1,1)$}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Case 2: $\omega^1=(9.5,9)$, $\omega^2=(0.5,1)$}} & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Equal weights $\lambda=\tfrac12$}} & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Unequal weights $\lambda\ne\tfrac12$; illustrate $\lambda=0.6$}} \\
\hline
\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(1) Setting.}} \emph{Objective:} each agent $h=1,2$ solves
$$ \max_{x_1^h,\,x_2^h\ge0}\ U^h(x_1^h,x_2^h)=\alpha\,x_1^h+\ln x_2^h,\qquad \alpha=1. $$
\emph{Choice variables:} $x_1^h,x_2^h$. Good $1$ is the \textcolor{orange}{numeraire} ($p_1=1$): utility \emph{linear} in $x_1$, so $MU_1=\alpha$ is constant. \emph{Constraints (multipliers):}
$$ p_1 x_1^h+p_2 x_2^h = w^h := p_1\omega_1^h+p_2\omega_2^h \quad(\lambda^h), \qquad x_1^h\ge0\ (\mu_1^h),\qquad x_2^h\ge0\ (\mu_2^h). $$
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} BC binds for sure (monotonicity, $\lambda^h>0$); $x_2^h>0$ slack for sure ($\ln\Rightarrow$ Inada); $x_1^h\ge0$ \textcolor{orange}{TO BE TESTED} (QL: no Inada) --- trial in (3), tested in (7).
\emph{Two endowment configurations, same aggregate $\omega=(10,10)$:}
$\bullet$ \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Case 1:}} $\omega^1=(9,\,9)$, $\omega^2=(1,\,1)$.
$\bullet$ \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Case 2:}} $\omega^1=(9.5,\,9)$, $\omega^2=(0.5,\,1)$.} & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(1) Write the planner problem.}} With $\lambda=\tfrac12$, multiplying the objective by $2$ does not affect the solution:
$$
\max_{x_1^1,x_1^2,x_2^1,x_2^2}
\;
x_1^1+\ln x_2^1+x_1^2+\ln x_2^2
$$
subject to
$$
x_1^1+x_1^2\le10,\qquad
x_2^1+x_2^2\le10,
$$
$$
x_1^1,x_1^2,x_2^1,x_2^2\ge0.
$$
Individual endowments do not enter the planner problem.
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} Resource constraints bind for sure (monotonicity, $\mu_1,\mu_2>0$); $x_2^h>0$ slack ($\ln$); $x_1^h\ge0$ \textcolor{orange}{TO BE TESTED} (linear) --- trial in (3), tested in (8). & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(1) Write the planner problem.}} With $\lambda\in(0,1)$:
$$
\max_{x_1^1,x_1^2,x_2^1,x_2^2}
\;
\lambda(x_1^1+\ln x_2^1)
+(1-\lambda)(x_1^2+\ln x_2^2)
$$
subject to
$$
x_1^1+x_1^2\le10,\qquad
x_2^1+x_2^2\le10,
$$
$$
x_1^1,x_1^2,x_2^1,x_2^2\ge0.
$$
Individual endowments do not enter the planner problem.
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} Resource constraints bind for sure (monotonicity, $\mu_1,\mu_2>0$); $x_2^h>0$ slack ($\ln$); $x_1^h\ge0$ \textcolor{orange}{TO BE TESTED} (linear) --- trial in (3), tested in (8). \\
\hline
\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(2) Lagrangian.}}
$$ \mathcal{L}^h=\alpha\,x_1^h+\ln x_2^h-\lambda^h\bigl(p_1 x_1^h+p_2 x_2^h-w^h\bigr)+\mu_1^h x_1^h+\mu_2^h x_2^h. $$} & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(2) Write the Lagrangian.}} $$
\mathcal L
=
x_1^1+\ln x_2^1+x_1^2+\ln x_2^2
+\mu_1(10-x_1^1-x_1^2)
+\mu_2(10-x_2^1-x_2^2)
$$
$$
+\nu_1^1x_1^1+\nu_1^2x_1^2
+\nu_2^1x_2^1+\nu_2^2x_2^2.
$$ & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(2) Write the Lagrangian.}} $$
\mathcal L
=
\lambda(x_1^1+\ln x_2^1)
+(1-\lambda)(x_1^2+\ln x_2^2)
+\mu_1(10-x_1^1-x_1^2)
+\mu_2(10-x_2^1-x_2^2)
$$
$$
+\nu_1^1x_1^1+\nu_1^2x_1^2
+\nu_2^1x_2^1+\nu_2^2x_2^2.
$$ \\
\hline
\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(3) FOCs for $x_1^h$ + CS (interior guess).}}
$$ \partial x_1^h:\ \ \alpha-\lambda^h p_1+\mu_1^h=0, $$
$$ \text{CS:}\ \ \mu_1^h x_1^h=0,\qquad \mu_2^h x_2^h=0. $$
\emph{Interior guess} ($x_1^h,x_2^h>0\Rightarrow\mu_1^h=\mu_2^h=0$ by CS --- \textbf{to be verified ex post}):
$$ \partial x_1^h\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{\textcolor{blue}{\lambda^h=\frac{\alpha}{p_1}=1}}\quad\text{\emph{pins the shadow value, NOT }} x_1^h\ \text{(linearity!)}. $$} & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(3) FOCs for $x_1^1,x_1^2$.}}
 Guess
$$
x_1^1,x_1^2,x_2^1,x_2^2>0.
$$
By CS,
$$
\nu_1^1=\nu_1^2=\nu_2^1=\nu_2^2=0.
$$
 $$
\partial x_1^1:
\quad
1-\mu_1=0,
$$
$$
\partial x_1^2:
\quad
1-\mu_1=0.
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{\textcolor{blue}{\mu_1=1}}.
$$
The two FOCs are mutually consistent, but they do not pin down the individual $x_1^h$ because utility is linear in $x_1$. & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(3) FOCs for $x_1^1,x_1^2$.}}
Guess
$$
x_1^1,x_1^2,x_2^1,x_2^2>0.
$$
By CS,
$$
\nu_1^1=\nu_1^2=\nu_2^1=\nu_2^2=0.
$$

$$
\partial x_1^1:
\quad
\lambda-\mu_1=0,
$$ $$
\partial x_1^2:
\quad
(1-\lambda)-\mu_1=0.
$$
Therefore the interior guess would require
$$
\mu_1=\lambda
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mu_1=1-\lambda.
$$
Hence
$$
\lambda=1-\lambda
\iff

$$

 \\
\hline
\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(4) FOCs for $x_2^h$.}}
$$ \partial x_2^h:\ \ \frac{1}{x_2^h}-\lambda^h p_2+\mu_2^h=0, $$
$$ \partial x_2^h\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{1}{x_2^h}=\lambda^h p_2\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{\textcolor{green}{x_2^{h*}=\frac{1}{p_2}}}. $$} & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(4) FOCs for $x_2^1,x_2^2$.}} Since $\ln x_2^h$ implies $x_2^h>0$, the $x_2$ choices are interior:

\quad

\quad

Thus

and therefore
$$
\boxed{\textcolor{green}{x_2^1=x_2^2}}.
$$ & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(4) FOCs for $x_2^1,x_2^2$.}} Since $\ln x_2^h$ implies $x_2^h>0$, the $x_2$ choices are interior:
$$
\partial x_2^1:
\quad
\frac{\lambda}{x_2^1}-\mu_2=0,
$$
$$
\partial x_2^2:
\quad
\frac{1-\lambda}{x_2^2}-\mu_2=0.
$$
Thus
$$
x_2^1=\frac{\lambda}{\mu_2},
\qquad
x_2^2=\frac{1-\lambda}{\mu_2},
$$
and therefore
$$
\boxed{\textcolor{green}{
\frac{x_2^1}{x_2^2}
=
\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}

$$ \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(5) Market clearing for $x_2$  $\Rightarrow$ price.}} Under the interior guess both agents demand $x_2^{h*}=1/p_2$:
$$ \sum_h x_2^{h*}=\frac{2}{p_2}=\omega_2=10 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\textcolor{blue}{p_2=\frac15=0.2}}. $$
\emph{(The $x_1$ market then clears by Walras' law.)}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(6) Marshallian demands.}} From the FOC ratio + binding budget:
$$ \boxed{\textcolor{green}{\ x_2^{h*}(p)=\frac{1}{p_2}\ \ \text{(wealth-independent)},\qquad x_1^{h*}(p,w^h)=w^h-p_2\,x_2^{h*}=w^h-1\ \ \text{(residual)}.\ }} $$

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(7) Ex-post interiority check.}}
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(a) Wealths at the candidate price $p_2=0.2$.}} $w^1=9+0.2\cdot9=10.8$; \quad $w^2=1+0.2\cdot1=1.2$.
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(b) Check $x_1^h=w^h-1>0$.}} $x_1^1=9.8>0$ ✓; \quad $x_1^2=0.2>0$ ✓. \textbf{Both interior --- the guess survives, the candidate CE stands.}
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(c) Re-solve with the corner.}} Not needed. & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(5) Market clearing for $x_2$  $\Rightarrow$ price.}} Under the interior guess both agents demand $x_2^{h*}=1/p_2$:
$$ \sum_h x_2^{h*}=\frac{2}{p_2}=\omega_2=10 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\textcolor{black}{p_2=\frac15=0.2}}. $$
\emph{(The $x_1$ market then clears by Walras' law.)}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(6) Marshallian demands.}} From the FOC ratio + binding budget:
$$ \boxed{\textcolor{green}{\ x_2^{h*}(p)=\frac{1}{p_2}\ \ \text{(wealth-independent)},\qquad x_1^{h*}(p,w^h)=w^h-p_2\,x_2^{h*}=w^h-1\ \ \text{(residual)}.\ }} $$

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(7) Ex-post interiority check.}}
$w^1=9.5+0.2\cdot9=11.3$; \quad $w^2=0.5+0.2\cdot1=0.7$.
$x_1^1=10.3>0$ ✓; \quad \textcolor{red}{$x_1^2=0.7-1=-0.3<0$ ✗ --- \textbf{interiority FAILS for agent 2}}: he cannot afford $x_2^*=5$ and a positive $x_1$. Corner: $x_1^2=0$, $\mu_1^2>0$.
Now:

$$ \frac{1}{p_2}+\frac{0.5+p_2}{p_2}=10\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{1.5}{p_2}+1=10\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{\textcolor{blue}{p_2=\frac16}}. $$ & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(5) Market Clearing for $x_2$ .}} Since utility is strictly increasing in $x_2^h$,

 \\
\hline
\multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EX-POST VERIFICATION (KKT).}} \textcolor{red}{Inada conditions could NOT be applied to the quasilinear good $x_1$ (they hold only for $\ln x_2$), so interiority is NOT guaranteed --- the FOC candidate must be verified: $x_1,x_2>0$ in columns 1 and 3; $x_1^2=0$ in columns 2 and 4.} \textcolor{orange}{This is an optimality check on the guess --- separate from market clearing, nothing to do with it!}} \\

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(11) Verify interiority: $x_1,x_2>0$ --- \textcolor{orange}{separate from market clearing (nothing to do with it!)}.}} INADA DOES NOT APPLY TO QL GOODS SO YOU NEED TO DO THIS: $x_1^{1*}=9.8>0$ ✓; \quad $x_1^{2*}=0.2>0$ ✓; \quad $x_2^{h*}=5>0$ ✓ ($\ln$ forces it). The interior guess is confirmed.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(12) Takeaway.}} \textcolor{orange}{Same $x_2=5$ across agents; the wealth difference is absorbed entirely by the numeraire} ($9.8$ vs $0.2$): Marshallian wealth-independence holds. & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(10) Final CE allocation.}} Wealths at $p_2=\tfrac16$: $w^1=9.5+\tfrac{9}{6}=11$, $w^2=0.5+\tfrac16=\tfrac23$.
$$ \boxed{\textcolor{blue}{\ \hat p=(1,\,\tfrac16),\quad}\ \textcolor{green}{\hat x^1=(10,\,6),\quad \hat x^2=(0,\,4).\ }} $$
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(11) Verify the corner: $x_1^2=0$ (and $x_1^1,x_2>0$) --- \textcolor{orange}{separate from market clearing (nothing to do with it!)}.}} $x_1^{1*}=10>0$ ✓; \quad $x_2^{1*}=6>0$, $x_2^{2*}=4>0$ ✓. KKT at the corner: $\lambda^2$ from the $x_2$ FOC: $\lambda^2=\dfrac{1/x_2^2}{p_2}=\dfrac{1/4}{1/6}=1.5$; then $\mu_1^2=\lambda^2 p_1-\alpha=0.5>0$ with $x_1^2=0$ --- \textcolor{orange}{CS consistent ✓.}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(12) Takeaway.}} \textcolor{red}{Wealth-independence breaks at the corner}: different $x_2$ (6 vs 4). The corner agent demands \emph{less} $x_2$ than at interior, so at $p_2=0.2$ there is excess supply $\Rightarrow$ the price must \emph{fall} to $p_2=\tfrac16$ to clear. & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(10) Final planner allocation.}} $$
\boxed{\textcolor{green}{
x^{1*}=(a,5),\qquad
x^{2*}=(10-a,5),
\qquad
0\le a\le10.
}}
$$
For example, choosing $a=9.8$:
$$
x^{1*}=(9.8,5),\qquad
x^{2*}=(0.2,5).
$$

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(11) Verify interiority: $x_1,x_2>0$ --- \textcolor{orange}{separate from market clearing (nothing to do with it!)}.}} $x_2^{1*}=x_2^{2*}=5>0$ ✓; \quad $x_1^{1*}=a\ge0$ and $x_1^{2*}=10-a\ge0$ for every $a\in[0,10]$ ✓ (strictly interior for $a\in(0,10)$; the endpoints are still KKT-consistent since $\nu_1^h=0$). The interior guess is confirmed. & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(10) Final planner allocation.}} For $\lambda=0.6$:
$$
\boxed{\textcolor{green}{
x^{1*}=(10,6),\qquad
x^{2*}=(0,4).
}}
$$
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(11) Verify the corner: $x_1^2=0$ and $x_2>0$ --- \textcolor{orange}{separate from market clearing (nothing to do with it!)}.}} $x_1^{1*}=10>0$ ✓; \quad $x_2^{1*}=6>0$, $x_2^{2*}=4>0$ ✓. Corner: from $\partial x_1^2$: $(1-\lambda)-\mu_1+\nu_1^2=0\ \Rightarrow\ \nu_1^2=\mu_1-(1-\lambda)=0.6-0.4=0.2>0$ with $x_1^2=0$ --- \textcolor{orange}{CS consistent ✓.}
 \\

nodes.title: Mechanism
nodes.content:
Mechanism: 

\textbf{Bang-for-buck adjustment.}
\textbf{1)} Quasilinear exrernality $\Rightarrow$ adding a negative externality to agent 1 shifts his (social) curve \emph{down}: his demand falls and the crossing drops \emph{below} the numeraire bang for buck line $\lambda / p_x$ (point $g$).
\textbf{2)} MRS imbalance (not optimal) (think at the bang for buck plot) => Price adjusts for markets to clear $\Rightarrow$ both bang for buck curves shift \emph{up} (in the bang for buck plot). So notice how as MB goes down P needs to go down for markets to clear! Two cases: 
2A. one sided externality, price goes down, but not to 0, and the other agents infinitely absorbs (excludign satiation) the good, the curves meet at the same level as before ($\lambda / p_x$) (column 1)
{{img:0|w=900}}

2B. Two sided externality, two options: i) price goes down and agents consume the same quantities!  (Pigou bites $\Leftrightarrow$ destruction occurs), applying a tax to everybody = applying a tax to nobody! Think about the planner: consumption for agent A and B was worth +40 for both. now after +40 of dabage we have +10.  Still, MB is positive, price geos down, markets clear, there is full consumption (column 3).But if the external damages differ across agents or depend differently on quantities, relative social MB changes and quantities will generally be reallocated.  ii) if price touches 0 MRS condition plot is no longer of interest, and there is destruction of the good! (column 4) 

\emph{Remark (agent 2 inelastic):} the price falls so much (by the full $d$) that agent 1 buys as much as before --- the price adjustment undoes the Pigou wedge.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{DESTRUCTION}}

\emph{Common setup.} $y$ is the externality good. 
$\bullet$ \textbf{QL symmetric:} $U^i=\ln y^i+x^i-y^{-i}$ (linear damage; both pollute).
$\bullet$ \textbf{QL asymmetric:} $U^1=\ln y^1+x^1$, \;\; $U^2=\ln y^2+x^2-y^1$ (only agent 1 pollutes).
$\bullet$ \textbf{Cobb--Douglas symmetric:} $U^i=\sqrt{x^i y^i}-y^{-i}$ (concave in both goods).

\emph{All five columns solve the same planner program below on the column's utilities; the \textbf{Symmetric RAW} column instead reports the uncorrected (CE-style) outcome, where each agent maximises ignoring the damage $-y^{-i}$ (so no $\mu_y$ wedge from the externality appears in its $y$-FOC).}
$$ \max_{\{y^i,x^i\}}\ \sum_i U^i \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_i y^i\le\omega_y\ (\mu_y),\ \ \sum_i x^i\le\omega_x\ (\mu_x),\ \ y^i,x^i\ge0. $$
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Binding status.}} $\sum_i x^i\le\omega_x$ binds for sure (monotone in $x$, $\mu_x>0$); $y^i,x^i\ge0$ slack in the cases below (Inada from $\ln$/$\sqrt{\cdot}$); $\sum_i y^i\le\omega_y$ \textcolor{orange}{TO BE TESTED} ($\mu_y\gtrless0$ is the whole point --- trial in step 3, check in step 5, re-solve in step 6).
\textbf{Lagrangian.} $$ \mathcal{L}=\sum_i U^i+\mu_y\Bigl(\omega_y-\sum_i y^i\Bigr)+\mu_x\Bigl(\omega_x-\sum_i x^i\Bigr). $$
\emph{Rows 1--2 of the table are the FOCs $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x^i=0$ and $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial y^i=0$; row 3 imposes the binding $\sum_i y^i=\omega_y$.}

nodes.title: PUBLIC GOODS INTRO
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Taxonomy: rivalry $\times$ excludability.}}

\begin{tabular}{p{6cm}|p{16cm}|p{16cm}}
& \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Rivalrous}} \;\;(my consumption blocks yours) & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Non-rivalrous}} \;\;(same unit enjoyed simultaneously) \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Excludable}} \;\;(can charge a price) & \textbf{Private}: panino. \emph{I eat the panino, you don't; price $6$\,\euro.} & \textbf{Club}: private beach. \emph{Both lie on the sand simultaneously; $30$\,\euro\ entry excludes outsiders.} \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Non-excludable}} \;\;(cannot prevent access) & \textbf{Common pool}: fish in the sea. \emph{I catch a fish, you don't have that one; but cannot prevent you from fishing.} & \textbf{Public}: defence / fireworks. \emph{Iron dome blocks a missile $\Rightarrow$ both houses saved; cannot let only some missiles pass.} \\
\end{tabular}



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. Public good vs externality.}}  TWO THINGS THAT ARE TOTALLY DIFFERENT!

$\bullet$ \emph{Externality}: agents choose private $y^1, y^2$; spillover is the side-effect on the other's utility.

$\bullet$ \emph{Public good}: a single $y$ is produced and consumed identically by all. \textbf{Both agents enjoy the SAME $y$} --- the structural difference.
\textcolor{red}{Pollution = public bad.} Non-rivalrous (everyone breathes the same air), non-excludable. All consume the same amount.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. Production model.}} Devote $z$ units of the private good as input to produce $y$ units of public good:
$$ \underbrace{c(y)}_{\text{cost of producing y}} \; \le \; \underbrace{z}_{\text{units (eg dollars) you dedicate to the production of y}}, \qquad c(0) = 0, \quad c'(y) > 0. $$ Comments: 
- the first equation is just saying: we need to take somewhere the money that costs us to produce y! hence, we need to input enough  money.** Obviosuly the first equation will hold with equality.**
- c(y) is just the raw rate of tranformation, so how many y you can make with given z. So if for example z = 2 and  $c(y) = \tfrac{1}{2} y^2 \text{(convex})$. If you have z= 2 you cna produce 2 y, if you jave z = 4.5 you can produce y = 3. 
- $c'(y)=MRT_{y,x}=\text{additional units of private good }x\text{ required to produce one additional marginal unit of public good }y.$
- Cost curvature: \emph{Convex} ($c'' > 0$): \textbf{the second unit is more expensive than the first, the third more than the second, etc.} Diminishing marginal returns.

trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{D. Missing market (Coase).}}
Missign market framework: if you assign the property right the problem will be solved as agents negotiate. Coase: which side gets the right doesn't change the allocation, only distribution.

\emph{Setting: right to agent 2 (e.g.\ the fisher owns the river).} Agent 2 holds the right to a clean environment; he can sell permits to agent 1 at price $r$. y is gasoline. Let $z$ be the tradeable right (one permit $\leftrightarrow$ one unit of $y^1$). $z^d$ = agent 1's demand, $z^s$ = agent 2's supply. \emph{Agent 2 controls how much $y^1$ agent 1 can consume by choosing how much $z^s$ to issue.}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{1. Setting.}}
\emph{\textcolor{red}{Agent 1} (choice variables $y^1, z^d, x^1$).} \emph{Objective:} $\max\; U^1(y^1) + x^1$. \emph{Constraints (multipliers):}
$$ p_1\, y^1 + r\, z^d + x^1 = \underbrace{\omega_x^1 + p_1\, \omega_y^1}_{M_1} \quad(\lambda_1), \qquad y^1 \le z^d \quad(\xi_1). $$
\emph{\textcolor{red}{Agent 2} (choice variables $y^1, z^s, x^2$).} \emph{Objective:} $\max\; U^2(y^2) - \varphi(y^1) + x^2$. \emph{Constraints (multipliers):}
$$ p_2\, y^2 + x^2 = \underbrace{\omega_x^2 + p_1\, \omega_y^2}_{M_2} + r\, z^s \quad(\lambda_2), \qquad y^1 = z^s \quad(\xi_2). $$

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{2. Lagrangians.}}
$$ \mathcal{L}^1 = U^1(y^1) + x^1 - \lambda_1\bigl(p_1 y^1 + r z^d + x^1 - M_1\bigr) + \xi_1\bigl(z^d - y^1\bigr). $$
$$ \mathcal{L}^2 = U^2(y^2) - \varphi(y^1) + x^2 - \lambda_2\bigl(p_2 y^2 + x^2 - M_2 - r z^s\bigr) + \xi_2\bigl(y^1 - z^s\bigr). $$

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{3. FOCs.}}
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Agent 1's FOCs.}}
in fixing y1, agent 1 has to anticipate how much r he will have to pay to agent 2 to buy y1
$$
\partial \mathcal{L}^1/\partial x^1:\;\; 1 - \lambda_1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\lambda_1 = 1},
$$
$$
\partial \mathcal{L}^1/\partial z^d:\;\; -\lambda_1 r + \xi_1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\xi_1 = r},
$$
$$
\partial \mathcal{L}^1/\partial y^1:\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} - \lambda_1 p_1 - \xi_1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} = p_1 + r}.
$$
the last equation is giving you the optimal $y^1$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Agent 2's FOCs.}}
in fixing r, agent 2 has to anticipate how much y1 agent 1 will ask for.
$$
\partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial x^2:\;\; 1 - \lambda_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\lambda_2 = 1},
$$
$$
\partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial y^2:\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^2} - \lambda_2 p_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^2} = p_2},
$$
$$
\partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial z^s:\;\; \lambda_2 r - \xi_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\xi_2 = r},
$$
$$
\partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial y^1:\;\; -\,\varphi'(y^1) + \xi_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{ r = \varphi'(y^1)}.
$$
Last equation is saying: that guy consumpion is creating this cost to me
Penultimate equation is saying: if you give that guy a permit, we sell until the mb of sellign = mc we are receiving.

the higehr the price (r) the higher the supply and the higher the demand. note that higher price at the margin here implies also higher marginal cost at the marhin. Note that if p up by 20% at the margin and c up by 20% at the margin, we are all happy and we maek more money. also because this is a marhin cnditio (the extra price you are getting on each unit, the extra cost is equal to the extra price just for the last unit). ALE IF YOU HAVE TIME SEARCH MORE ON WHY A PRICE INCREASE EQUAL TO A MARGINAL COST INCREASE IS ALWAYS PROFITALE.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Market-clearing.}}
standard consitions plus on top:  $z^d = z^s$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why D beats A, B, C.}} The market \textbf{discovers $r^*$ endogenously} through agent 2's supply decision. \emph{The planner does NOT need to know $\varphi'(y^{1*})$ ex ante} --- agent 2 reveals it through his FOC for selling permits. Pigou (B), subsidy (C), and quota (A) all require the planner to compute $\varphi'$ in advance; D escapes this informational burden.

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Coase caveats:}} (i) property rights must be well-defined and enforceable, (ii) transaction costs must be low, (iii) breaks with many parties / asymmetric info.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(6) Two characterizations of Pareto Set (PS).}}

\emph{Why a planner?} Both characterizations are written from the viewpoint of a benevolent social planner who chooses an allocation $(x_h^1,x_l^1,x_h^2,x_l^2)\in\mathcal F$ to maximize a welfare objective. Two possible characterizations:

{{img:0|w=580}}

\begin{tabular}{p{3.1cm}|p{9cm}|p{9cm}}
& \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{[A] Linear scalarization --- weighted SWF}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{[B] Constrained maximization --- UPF as a function}} \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{1. Setting.}} \emph{(objective, choice variables)} &
\emph{Objective:} $\max\ \lambda U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)+(1-\lambda)U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2)$. \emph{Choice variables:} $x_h^1,x_l^1,x_h^2,x_l^2\ge0$. \emph{Weight} $\lambda\in(0,1)$ fixed; varying it traces the frontier. &
\emph{Objective:} $P(\bar u^1)=\max\ U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2)$ --- fix agent 1 at a utility floor and push agent 2 up. \emph{Choice variables:} $x_h^1,x_l^1,x_h^2,x_l^2\ge0$. \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{2. Constraints (multipliers).}} &
Resource feasibility only:
$$ x_h^1+x_h^2=\omega_h\ (\mu_h),\qquad x_l^1+x_l^2=\omega_l\ (\mu_l). $$ &
Utility floor plus resource feasibility:
$$ U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)\ge\bar u^1\ (\gamma),\quad x_h^1+x_h^2=\omega_h\ (\mu_h),\quad x_l^1+x_l^2=\omega_l\ (\mu_l). $$ \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{3. Lagrangian.}} &
$$ \mathcal L=\lambda U^1+(1-\lambda)U^2+\mu_h(\omega_h-x_h^1-x_h^2)+\mu_l(\omega_l-x_l^1-x_l^2). $$ &
$$ \mathcal L=U^2+\gamma\bigl(U^1-\bar u^1\bigr)+\mu_h(\omega_h-x_h^1-x_h^2)+\mu_l(\omega_l-x_l^1-x_l^2). $$ \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{4. FOCs} (one per choice variable).} &
$$ \lambda\tfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_h^1}=\mu_h,\qquad \lambda\tfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_l^1}=\mu_l, $$
$$ (1-\lambda)\tfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_h^2}=\mu_h,\qquad (1-\lambda)\tfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_l^2}=\mu_l. $$ &
$$ \tfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_h^2}=\mu_h,\qquad \tfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_l^2}=\mu_l, $$
$$ \gamma\tfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_h^1}=\mu_h,\qquad \gamma\tfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_l^1}=\mu_l. $$ \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{5. Result} (Pareto condition).} &
$$ \boxed{\ \mathrm{MRS}^1_{h,l}=\tfrac{\mu_h}{\mu_l}=\mathrm{MRS}^2_{h,l}\ } $$ &
The \emph{same} condition, with $\gamma$ playing the role of the weight ratio $\dfrac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}$. Both approaches deliver the identical Pareto-efficiency condition. \\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{purple}{Reading [A] --- isowelfare geometry.}}
- Note how in the isowelfare space the welfare line $ W = \lambda U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1) +(1-\lambda)U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2)$, solving for $U^2$, has slope $-\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda},$ and its vertical intercept is $ K=\frac{W}{1-\lambda}.$ For a fixed value of $\lambda$, maximizing welfare means moving the isowelfare line outward, parallel to itself, until it reaches the utility-possibility set. The highest attainable isowelfare line determines the planner's optimum. If the utility-possibility set is compact and the weighted welfare function is continuous, the Weierstrass theorem guarantees that a maximum exists. This means that, for every fixed $\lambda$, the weighted social-welfare problem has at least one solution (a PO point, again, existence of a PO point is easy).
- Remark: you need $\lambda \in (0,1)$ since we could have agent i satiation. In case of strict monotonicity this would not be needed
- Varying $\lambda$ traces the supported points of the utility-possibility frontier.

Note how beautiful the math is: the common rhs allows you to unify the utility you give to agent 1 to the utility you give to agent 2. This means that $\mu_h$ is gonna be the unified value of consuming good h and $\mu_l$ the unified value of consuming good l. Obviously dependign on the weights and the utility functions the level of these thresholds will change! In the end, you will reach the welfare enhancing marginal value of consumption of the two goods, you will have to let agents consume up to these unified values.

This conditions tells you what is the optimal rate of change of good h for good l

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{[B] traces the UPF.}} Thus, the constrained-maximization approach gives the same Pareto-efficiency condition as the weighted social-welfare approach. The planner fixes Agent 1 at a utility floor $\bar u^1$ and maximizes Agent 2's utility. By varying $\bar u^1$ over its feasible range,
$$
\bar u^1\in[u_{\min}^1,u_{\max}^1],
$$
the planner traces the utility-possibility frontier as an explicit decreasing function $U^2=P(U^1).$

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Example --- one-good economy.}}

Suppose there is only one good, with total endowment $\omega$, and that $U^i$ is strictly increasing for each agent. Since there is only one good, denote the amount consumed by Agent $i$ simply by $x^i$. The constrained-maximization problem becomes
$$
P(\bar u^1)
=
\max_{x^1,x^2\geq0}
U^2(x^2)
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
U^1(x^1)\geq\bar u^1,
\qquad
x^1+x^2=\omega.
$$

- Strict monotonicity implies that Agent 1's utility constraint binds: $ U^1(x^1)=\bar u^1.$ Therefore $x^1=(U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1).$

- Resource feasibility implies $ x^2 = \omega-x^1 = \omega-(U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1). $

Hence, $\boxed{ P(\bar u^1) = U^2\left( \omega-(U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1) \right)}$

\textbf{Prices and trade in a one-good exchange economy.}

In the two-good economy, the general budget constraint of Agent $i$ is $p_hx_h^i+p_lx_l^i = p_h\omega_h^i+p_l\omega_l^i.$ In a one-good economy, the budget constraint becomes $px^i=p\omega^i $

For any strictly positive price $p>0$, $ x^i=\omega^i $

Thus, each agent can afford only their initial endowment. There is no relative price because there is only one good, and setting $p=1$ is merely a numéraire normalization.

The relevant statement is not that the budget line has slope one: with only one good, the budget set is a point on a one-dimensional consumption space rather than a line in a two-dimensional diagram.

trash.title: Value of information --- setting and Bayesian updating
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setting.}}

A decision maker (DM) --- think of a \emph{judge} --- faces uncertainty over a binary state $\omega \in \Omega = \{I, G\}$ ($I$ = innocent, $G$ = guilty). His belief is summarized by the scalar
$$\mu \;=\; \Pr(\omega = G) \;\in\; [0,1].
$$

$\bullet$ $\mu = 1$: certain guilt. $\bullet$ $\mu = 0$: certain innocence. $\bullet$ $\mu = 1/2$: maximal uncertainty.

The judge picks an action $a \in \mathscr{A} = \{A, C\}$ (acquit or convict). Payoffs match action to state: $u = 1$ if he ``gets it right'' and $0$ otherwise.

\textbf{Payoff table $u(a,\omega)$:}

\begin{tabular}{p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}}
$u(a,\omega)$ & $I$ & $G$ \\
\hline
$A$ & $1$ & $0$ \\
\hline
$C$ & $0$ & $1$ \\
\end{tabular}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Expected utility of each action (as a function of belief).}}

\emph{Convict:} \;$U(C,\mu) \;=\; (1-\mu)\,\underbrace{u(C,I)}_{=\,0} \;+\; \mu\,\underbrace{u(C,G)}_{=\,1} \;=\; \mu.$

\emph{Acquit:} \;$U(A,\mu) \;=\; (1-\mu)\,\underbrace{u(A,I)}_{=\,1} \;+\; \mu\,\underbrace{u(A,G)}_{=\,0} \;=\; 1-\mu.$

So $U(C,\cdot)$ is linear with slope $+1$ (rewards belief in guilt), and $U(A,\cdot)$ is linear with slope $-1$ (rewards belief in innocence). Plotted together, they form an \textbf{X-shape} crossing at $\mu = 1/2$.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Optimal action and value function.}}

The judge picks whichever action has higher expected payoff:
$$
a^*(\mu) \;=\; \begin{cases} A & \text{if } \mu \le \hat\mu = \tfrac{1}{2}, \\ C & \text{if } \mu \ge \hat\mu = \tfrac{1}{2}, \end{cases}
\qquad\text{with cutoff } \hat\mu = \tfrac{1}{2}.
$$

The associated maximised expected payoff --- the \textbf{value function} --- is
$$
\boxed{\;U(\mu) \;=\; \max\bigl\{\,U(C,\mu),\; U(A,\mu)\,\bigr\} \;=\; \max\{\mu,\; 1-\mu\}\;}
$$

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Plot: X-shape with convex upper envelope.}}

{{img:0|w=720}}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Reading: why is $U(\mu)$ convex (and what does it mean)?}}

$U(\mu)$ is the \emph{upper envelope of two linear functions} of $\mu$ $\Rightarrow$ automatically \textbf{convex}. Graphically: V-shape, minimum at the cutoff $\hat\mu = 1/2$, maxima at the corners $\mu = 0$ and $\mu = 1$.

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Important contrast with vNM utility.}} In standard vNM expected utility, $u$ is concave \emph{in wealth} (risk aversion). Here the value function $U$ is convex \emph{in belief}. Different objects, different reasons:

$\bullet$ \emph{vNM concavity in wealth}: averaging is bad --- a sure middle wealth beats a fair gamble between extremes (risk aversion).

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian convexity in belief}:  certainty at the corners ($\mu = 0$ or $\mu = 1$) means the DM \emph{knows the state} and picks the right action with payoff $1$. At $\mu = 1/2$ he is maximally confused and gets only $1/2$. \textbf{More information $\Rightarrow$ beliefs closer to corners $\Rightarrow$ better decisions $\Rightarrow$ higher expected payoff.} This convexity is exactly what will make the value of information non-negative in the next snippet. Effect: averaging on signals that bring you close to the tails is great!
